speechtext:
May I be permitted to make a short statement at this time? Yesterday, when the house was considering third reading of the bill in connection with the foot-and-mouth disease, Mr. Diefenbaker moved an amendment. The Minister of Agriculture contended that the amendment was out of order. However, I allowed it to stand.
Since that time I have given further consideration to the amendment, and although it may have been technically in order I am rather doubtful of the practical result which would have followed if it had carried. The committee would have reconsidered an amendment which would have necessitated an expenditure of money. But the committee could not have taken any action on the matter without a motion by a member of the government. The government had intimated that it would not propose such an amendment. Accordingly I am doubtful if any useful purpose would have been served by referring the matter back to the committee.
The purpose of this statement is to advise the house that, for the reasons which I have stated and for other reasons, should a similar amendment be moved on any future occasion, I would not feel myself bound by the ruling which I made yesterday.

speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the mover (Mr. George) and the seconder (Mr. Gauthier, Lake St. John) of this resolution in no merely formal spirit, but in the belief that they have very com-mendably accepted the responsibility imposed upon them. Each of them naturally dealt with the great advantages of his own part of the country. That, I think, is a healthy example of the kind of faith in one's own community which collectively builds a strong country. Naturally they would not expect every other hon. member to agree entirely with their estimate of the advantages of their own communities as against other communities in the country, but I do share with others who have expressed the same opinion that their task was performed in a manner that does credit to this house.
When this session opened a few days ago we paid our respects to the memory of a greatly loved king. We expressed our sorrow and sympathy for the members of his family in his sudden death, and we expressed our loyalty to his daughter who has now become our queen. It is a period of mourning and also of dedication. As we remember the fortitude, simplicity and kindness with which he undertook his many and heavy duties, we are reminded of the strength of those virtues which he exemplified and of the immense power exercised by the unquestioned goodness of this saintly man. By the unselfishness and devotion to his own tasks there

comes to each one of us a challenge to dedicate ourselves to the task of maintaining and strengthening in every way within our power, by thought, word and deed, those cherished institutions which he served so well.
It is in this solemn atmosphere that we now examine the first speech from the throne delivered to the parliament of Canada in the reign of Queen Elizabeth II. The solemnity of the occasion and its historic significance in no way change the recognized fact that the speech from the throne is simply the statement of the government which outlines its plans for the coming session. It is read by Her Majesty's representative in the exact form prepared by the government itself. It is in that light, and in that light alone, that it must be examined today as it has been the custom to examine the speech from the throne in this and other legislative assemblies which follow the same parliamentary practices.
The members of this house will all give their enthusiastic approval to the expressions of loyalty which it contains. There are other announcements also which will be welcomed. All members will indeed agree that the Canadian forces in Korea are serving in a manner which gives Canadians today new reason to be proud of the character and fortitude of their young men and women.
While the road to general peace and real international security is bound to be long and hard, there have been encouraging signs that the free nations, and particularly the nations of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, have been working in closer harmony and with an increasing sense of reality.
The Lisbon conference may well have been a turning point in history. The decision to have one integrated army, which would wear the same uniform as the evidence of its unity, may well prove decisive in the years ahead. It would also seem that a much more realistic atmosphere pervaded the meeting than has been apparent at any time in the past.
If the meetings were realistic, however, the statement issued by the meeting was the very contrary. It was bad from the international point of view; it was bad from the point of view of our own people, and, above all, it was bad because it gave assurances which were not based on facts. It is difficult to understand what would prompt those responsible for such a statement to announce that there would be fifty divisions in the European army by the end of this year. If we were to accept a statement of that kind we would simply be deluding ourselves. Most certainly it will not fool the Russians.
The Address-Mr. Drew
Bad though that statement is, it justifies in no way the amazing declaration of policy issued the day before yesterday to the press by the socialist party. Having very correctly pointed out the unsatisfactory nature of the statement issued from Lisbon, there can be no justification for the suggestion that Canada should oppose the armament goals set at Lisbon. Those who have been reading press reports of numbers of communist divisions, the quality and numbers of Russian jet aircraft and the new Russian jet bomber, to say nothing of their more recent advances in tank design, should be well aware that our sights must not be set lower, but much higher in terms of real hitting power. What we need, and need desperately in the shortest possible time, is some rationalization of military contribution to the common cause which will make the maximum use of the tremendous industrial potential on this continent and at the same time make effective use of the vast pool of available manpower in Europe. In this there is no suggestion that Canada should in any respect shirk its duties and its responsibilities. But transportation over thousands of miles, and the feeding, equipping and maintaining of armed men, does suggest the application of simple military logistics to this problem. These are subjects, however, to be discussed in detail at another time.
I did not think I should let pass unnoticed this unfortunate declaration of policy by the socialist party, which combines anti-American sentiment with anti-military demands in words which have a surprising similarity to those employed by the irresponsible element of the socialist party in Britain. It is reassuring to know that those dangerous policies were so decisively repudiated by the socialist party in Britain the day before yesterday. I earnestly hope they do not represent the attitude of the socialist members in this house, because their statements in the past have expressed a different point of view.
Even though the statement issued from the Lisbon conference so obviously overstates the extent of our combined arrangements for defence, this is more than balanced by extremely reassuring news of another kind. Very much more important than these overstatements, to which unfortunately we have become accustomed here in Canada, was the recent announcement that Britain has for some time been building and has completed a number of atom bombs. This will make a profound impression on the men in the Kremlin, and will overweigh many, many times the phantom divisions paraded at Lisbon.
Remembering that it was British research and British scientists who made possible the
15$	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Drew construction o f the first atom bombs, and that those same scientists are now back in Britain and have for some time been working on this project there, we need have no doubt that this new contribution to the military strength of the democracies is one which may well weigh the scales decisively on the side of peace.
I have mentioned this subject today for another reason. I trust that there is no thought that the statements in regard to the Lisbon conference and defence will be given by the ministers responsible, within the framework of this debate. The discussion of the Lisbon conference should be a separate debate, following the introduction of a resolution calling for approval of whatever it was the Canadian government agreed to undertake at that conference.
The discussion of defence, which will bring us up to date-or we hope it will-and also make it possible for us to discuss those aspects of defence outside the scope of the North Atlantic treaty organization, should be a separate debate. Both these debates should come on as soon as possible. If some indication were given of the time and the manner of their introduction, I am sure that the debate on the speech from the throne might be comparatively short, because the members would then know that we would soon be discussing subjects that are very much in their minds.
Now I shall refer to the speech from the throne itself.
The fact that the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Veterans Benefit Act are to be amended will be welcomed by those members who have long been pressing for improvement in this legislation, so that the veterans who depend upon the payments provided by those acts may receive some measure of that assistance which is long overdue in meeting the difficult financial position in which they have been placed, by events beyond their control.
Members on both sides of the house will also welcome the opportunity to bring our Criminal Code up to date and to carry out the adjustment of representation in the House of Commons, which is the obligation of parliament after each decennial census.
Beyond that there is nothing which appears to be of particular importance, and certainly nothing which has not already been indicated for some time in the discussions as to what we might expect at this session. It is as lean fare as has ever been placed before the members of this parliament.

It is to be most earnestly hoped that no legislation which the government now contemplates is being held back at this time to provide an excuse for a second session again this year. The effectiveness of this parliament will be greatly injured if that practice continues. The people of Canada are not unwilling to recognize the fact that members of parliament living away from home are put to unusual expense, and that in any event their membership in the House of Commons does impose heavy financial obligations upon them. But I am sure that the people of Canada, whose servants we are, would prefer to see that fact recognized in an appropriate manner, rather than to adopt a device which discourages many people from offering themselves for parliament because of the amount of time which must now be spent in Ottawa and the sense of frustration created by the planned ineffectiveness of extra sessions of that kind.
As an agenda of government business it is a most discouraging and uninformative statement. In fact, even in those cases where there is some appearance of an assurance of things to be done, there is no real information. We are left to guess that the amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Veterans Benefit Act will provide those increases in payments which we have been urging for so long. We are also left to guess what revisions there will be to the Immigration Act and to the Canadian Citizenship Act. May I say that we have an example before us at the present time which indicates that important and far-reaching amendments are actually needed. Even recognizing the practice of employing somewhat general statements in the speech from the throne, this speech must constitute an unchallenged record for ambiguity. Its importance lies not in what it says, but in what it omits to say.
If the government is planning any measures in keeping with the seriousness of the situation with which we are confronted, then the speech from the throne is hardly in keeping with the responsibility of the government to parliament and the people of Canada. If ever there was a speech from the throne which deserved severe criticism from both sides of the house, it is that now before us. The solemn events which we have already recalled in this house are no reason for limiting in any degree the vigour of the criticism which should be expressed. On the contrary, those events themselves, which have served to remind us of the strength of our continuing parliamentary institutions, should remind us also of the extent to which the strength of our democracy depends upon criticism. To

those who disapprove of criticism may I point out what has been said on this subject by the greatest living parliamentarian and perhaps the greatest parliamentarian who ever lived. These are the words of Winston Churchill:
Criticism in the body politic is like pain in the human body. It is not pleasant, but where would the body be without it? No health or sensibility would be possible without continued correctives and warnings of pain. It is in the fear of criticism that . . . dictatorships run their greatest risk. They silence all criticism by the concentration camp, the rubber truncheon, or the firing party. Thus the men at the top must very often only be fed with the facts which are palatable to them. Scandals, corruption, and shortcomings are not exposed, because there are no independent voices. Instead of being exposed, they continue to fester behind the pompous frontage of the state.
I trust that we shall always be found willing here in this house, no matter what party forms the government of this country, to co-operate in every way with the government in advancing legislation, or in any other parliamentary duty, where it appears that the government is acting in the best interests of the people of Canada. Here, as in other free lands, the opposition must insist upon its right and duty to penetrate and examine behind the pompous frontage of the state. What is sometimes forgotten by those who too readily criticize criticism itself is that in every session of parliament there is a very high measure of co-operation in regard to many of the matters that come before parliament. I think hon. members will agree that we have already seen an example of a practical measure of co-operation during the present session.
But at a time when the very existence of an opposition is in itself the clear hallmark of our parliamentary freedom, it is the duty of all members who do not agree with what the government is doing, or failing to do, to exercise their right of criticism. That applies to all members of the house, on whichever side of the Speaker they may sit. Some of the finest examples of parliamentary oratory and democracy are to be found in speeches made by those who have spoken from conviction against a government formed from the party to which they belong. There are no better examples of speeches of that kind than those of Winston Churchill himself. In recent years this house has not been furnished with any very striking examples of speeches of that kind. It would be refreshing and extremely helpful if we heard speeches during this debate, informing the government in the clearest possible terms that many of its supporters in parliament believe that their constituents want positive and immediate
The Address-Mr. Drew action to deal with subjects which are not given the respect of a passing glance in the speech from the throne.
What member of this house can be unaware that the people of every part of Canada are greatly concerned about the high cost of living, continuing inflation, crushing overtaxation, unemployment, and the loss of markets for our agricultural products? Yet where is there any reference to these subjects in the speech from the throne?
Inflation continues to mount, with resulting losses to the savings of our people. The heavy burden of overtaxation is felt indirectly or directly by all Canadians, and yet this, and the inflation which it helps to produce, receive only a passing reference in the casual statement that "inflationary pressures are still being strongly felt and require the maintenance of anti-inflationary measures". That is all. There is nothing more. No assurances whatever of any positive measures which might offer some hope of relief to our people at this time.
What about the very serious unemployment which is developing in some areas, and particularly amongst immigrants for whom no satisfactory placing arrangements have been made? No plans are indicated. This subject is completely ignored. In fact it is disregarded in the bland comment that "generally speaking employment remains at a high level".
What of the plight of our farmers, and particularly our dairy farmers, who now find their traditional markets greatly reduced, if not entirely closed? There is no indication of any plan which will give assurance to those farmers who depend upon export markets at a time when they are planning their production for the coming year. They are simply told that external trade has reached a record level.
If the speech from the throne is in fact an indication of the government's program for this session, it constitutes in itself an unanswerable indictment of this government's failure to meet the most urgent problems now confronting our people.
At the end of 1951 the cost of living in Canada had reached the highest figure in all our history. This is something of very real concern to every Canadian. It is a tragedy to a very large number of people on small fixed incomes or pensions. The few dollars available to them will buy considerably less than half the food the same number of dollars would have bought just before the war. And yet that was the time at which the level of a large number of these small incomes
160	HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Drew
was fixed. Many of the people in this unfortunate position are feeling the pinch more severely now than at any time in the past. A great many of them have sold their bonds or realized upon other savings which they had expected would protect them in their old age. Some of them have learned for the first time that the bonds which the government encouraged them to believe were the best and safest investment of all are now worth substantially less than their face value in dollars, and in real value perhaps no more than half of what they put into them.
Inflation is still the greatest challenge that we face, next to the possibility of war itself. From this side of the house we have been emphasizing that fact over and over again, and especially since the outbreak of the Korean war. Over and over again we have introduced resolutions demanding action by the government to hoi 1 down the cost of living and check inflation by every means within its power.
There was never any doubt about the inflationary pressures that would be created the moment it became necessary for us to divert large sums of money and resources, as well as manpower, for military purposes. In that respect the situation in Canada is not unique. The same thing happens in every country, because the withdrawal of manpower, of resources, and of industrial effort from peacetime activity invariably creates shortages which in turn bring with them inflationary pressures. But it is the duty of the government to take the appropriate steps which will check the inflation which is created by the very things that it is doing to defend our country and our economy. What we have urged over and over again is that, with their own officials and all the expert advice available to them in Canada, this government should take every possible step to balance the inflationary pressures with anti-inflationary checks and balances. That they have not done. Inflation has reached its highest point and the end is not yet. The welcome drop of a fraction of one point in the cost of living index announced the day before yesterday does not lessen the seriousness of the situation.
We have the unqualified statement of Mr. James Muir, president of the Royal Bank of Canada, in the annual statement to the shareholders of that bank on January 11, that "the third wave of inflationary pressure will come in full force upon us only when the rate of armament spending reaches its height". Those were the words of one of our most experienced and wise bankers.

We know that we have not yet reached that point. Effective steps have not been taken to deal with the inflation which we have already felt. This is not a statement made in this house merely for the purpose of seeking to cause discomfiture to the government. It has been made by many of the greatest experts on finance across Canada during the past few months. The speech from the throne offers no hope that adequate measures will be taken to meet this new and still more dangerous threat which could set off chain reactions which would be most difficult to control.
The government has been directly responsible for much of the inflation which we have already felt. The government has added to the great burden of our people by overtaxing them above the already heavy taxes by almost $700 million in the first nine months of the present fiscal year. Their own figures show a surplus for three-quarters of the year of $721,600,000, as against the $30 million surplus estimated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) when he obtained authority from parliament last year to impose the taxes for the current fiscal year.
There might be some thought that this is a subject to discuss when we have the new budget before us. I submit, however, that it is not only appropriate but our duty to deal with this subject now and not wait for the next budget, because the Minister of Finance has already made it clear that he does not regard overtaxation of this kind as inflationary. In fact he tells us that it is a splendid thing. That being the expressed opinion of the Minister of Finance, it is urgently necessary tc do our utmost to impress upon the government the need for a clear and positive declaration that it will abandon this strange and offensive policy, a policy which suggests that it is wise for the government to overtax our people so that the people may be protected from their own folly and the foolish spending of their own money.
Canadians are called upon to pay so much of their tax contributions in hidden and disguised forms that it is necessary from time to time to remind ourselves just what we actually are paying in taxes now. The current budget calls for tax levies of $3,730 million. So that we may realize in understandable terms what this means, it is well to remind ourselves that this is considerably in excess of the total gross value of all the products from our farms, forests, mines, fisheries and electric plants in the whole of Canada during 1950. When one thinks of all the human energy that went into production of that kind, the great basic production of the country, and sees that the

total value of all that production is less than the amount of taxes levied under the budget passed last year, one begins to realize something of the real load of taxes that our people are called upon to carry. That is the extent to which the money earned by our people is being withdrawn from their own control and channelled through- this vast bureaucracy.
To illustrate in the simplest way what this means to the individual, may I remind their representatives here that this amounts to more than $265 a year for every man, woman and child in Canada. To put it in another way, it means that through all the open and hidden forms of taxation the average payment of taxes called for by the current budget from the head of a family of five is now $1,325 for the one year.
On top of that Canadians have been overtaxed by approximately $700 million during the first nine months of the fiscal year. This amounts in overtaxation, above the figures of taxes I have given, to $50 a head, or $250 for the head of a family of five. That is what Canadians are now paying. If the government want to know where to tackle inflation first, let them cut off that overtaxation and reduce inflation by letting the people handle their own money with the wisdom that people have who know how hard it is to earn that money. That is the crushing load that should be eased. It is the crushing load that must be eased if the first and obvious step towards checking inflation is to be taken at all. At a time when unhappy events are making so many Canadians uneasy about the immediate future, -and we have been discussing some of those within the past few days-the government should give assurance without delay that this crippling load of taxation will be reduced. I hope we will receive that assurance from the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when he rises to speak in the house this afternoon.
That is the truly serious aspect of this question. Not only has it added directly to inflation; not only has it greatly increased the cost of living; not only has it hindered our export market by adding to the cost of our products, but it has been done without any authority from the people's representatives assembled in parliament.
The Minister of Finance told the people of Canada over the radio two weeks ago that he has used this overtaxation to make substantial payments on the public debt. He has pointed out that if no such surplus of this kind had occurred he would have been unable to make those payments. Does that mean that he thinks he was bound to make those payments? If it does, then it means that he did not disclose his plans to the members 55704-11
The Address-Mr. Drew of this house at the time he was asking permission to levy taxes on the people of Canada. It may be a fine thing to pay off debts at the appropriate time, but if it is the intention of the Minister of Finance to raise taxes for that purpose, it is his bounden duty to explain that fact to the members of parliament before a budget is passed which provides taxes of that kind.
This unauthorized overtaxation does not check inflation; it aggravates it. That has been stated by those who are responsible for the direction of some of our greatest financial institutions. This overtaxation is an inflationary time bomb with a delayed action fuse waiting to be touched off by the pressure of political advantage. Unless the government reconsiders its dangerous decision and acts immediately to withdraw the fuse the bomb could explode at a time when it would do irreparable damage to the economy of this country.
As we meet in this new session it is our urgent duty to insist that the business of the people be returned to the real control of the parliament of Canada. The last budget represents the worst miscalculation in Canadian history, which would for all time challenge the accuracy and reliability of any future financial statement of this government. Or on the other hand it was a defiant deception of parliament. It was one or the other; it could be nothing else. The statement of the Minister of Finance over the radio two weeks ago almost sounded as though at all times he had recognized the need for such a surplus. Surely he is not suggesting that he came before the house last year knowing he was going to need money for this purpose, and hid this information from the members of parliament without whose authority he has no right to levy a single cent in taxation. Unfortunately it reminds us of a statement which cannot be easily forgotten: "If we want to get away with it, who is going to stop us?"
One of the things which makes the present total of overtaxation so inexcusable is the fact that during the budget debate last spring the minister was warned over and over again against the effect of the regressive sales tax, which he increased by twenty-five per cent, and also the serious effect of the present excise tax on such essential household requirements as electric stoves, refrigerators and other things of that kind. The minister was also warned of the effect of the unnecessary taxes he was imposing on automobiles, cigarettes and other things which may be regarded by some as luxuries but which are now in such general use that the effect of

The Address-Mr. Drew such taxation inevitably results in a very substantial over-all increase in the cost of living. In fact it would appear that his own constituents have indicated to him their views about some aspects of taxation of that kind. In view of that fact, even if the minister may not become more responsive to the views expressed in this house, we hope he may give appropriate recognition to the expressed opinion of the constituents whom he is called upon to serve.

speechtext:
One of the things which makes this overtaxation so inexcusable is the fact that when these warnings were issued last year he treated them with an airy disregard and made no attempt to bring forward sound arguments against the constructive proposals and resolutions that were put forward.
There has never been any argument from this side of the house that some credit restrictions were not desirable. But there is a vast difference between credit restrictions which reduce unnecessary purchases when there is a shortage of materials, and credit restrictions so severe that they prevent the purchase of things which have become essential requirements in our complex daily life. There are medicines which may be very, good for particular ailments, but which taken in excess may kill the patient. To some extent that is what has been happening in a number of cases, having regard to the way in which the government has handled credit restrictions. Those restrictions have been made so severe as to create unemployment simply by blocking sales.
While it is in the budget that we shall receive an explanation of the details of taxes for the next year, we should have had assurances at this time that the government does intend to remove some of these wholly unnecessary nuisance taxes which have created unemployment, hindered the building of new houses, increased inflation, and in many cases prevented the purchase of things

that are now regarded as necessities and for which there were adequate supplies of raw materials.
Moreover, there is no assurance of any real attempt to check government extravagance and reduce non-defence expenditures. Last year the Minister of Finance told us the government was reversing the upward trend of non-defence expenditures. The fact is that for the first nine months of the fiscal year, instead of the promised reduction of some $35 million in those expenditures there has been an increase of $37,400,000.
In the case of defence expenditures there is much to be explained. The men and women in the uniform of our army, navy and air force give us good reason for pride in the spirit and character of young Canadians; but what have we to show for the enormous expenditures which have been made? There will be other opportunities to discuss this question in detail, and, as I have said before, I hope it will be in a separate debate on this subject where the discussion can be integrated. But if the added commitments undertaken at NATO are approved, and we consider those expenses on top of what is already being spent for national defence, we must ask ourselves what would happen to our economy if we became involved in any more extended commitments and expenses increased on a proportionate basis. For that reason I ask now, while I am speaking in this debate, that the committee on defence expenditures be set up immediately so that a real inquiry may be undertaken into those expenditures which are bearing most heavily upon the taxpayers of Canada.
I have spoken of unemployment. It is being greatly aggravated by unplanned immigration, by bringing newcomers to Canada without adequate organization to assist them in finding jobs. The large number of unemployed immigrants now gathered outside Toronto, Montreal and other large cities are not only adding to our unemployment problem, but, as the weeks and months drag by without an opportunity being afforded them to obtain steady jobs, the seeds are being sown for future discontent and bitterness in the minds of people who were encouraged to come here in the belief that they 'would have work as soon as they arrived. I am sure those people are people who can and will make as fine citizens as this country wants. But we ourselves must not be those responsible for planting in them the seeds of suspicion and distrust of this democracy of ours.
What has happened to the manpower committee, the committee that was supposed to deal with all these things? Manpower,

employment and immigration are all directly related. That committee is so loaded with government officials that the businessmen who were asked to serve on it seem to have had little opportunity to make any effective plans for the full use of the manpower of this country. If they have had the opportunity, then it has not been put into written form at any time.
That committee, I submit, should be reconstituted with no government officials on it. The officials-men who are fully capable of giving the information required and of supplying the necessary details-should be available at all times, but they should be available for that purpose and should not be the ones to decide what the committee will say as to the manpower situation in this country. The duties of that committee should be extended to the general problem of unemployment and the consideration of plans for properly selecting, screening and placing immigrants coming into this country. May I say that although I have advocated immigration, and sought to assist immigration of a selected type at the time I had some responsibility for that matter, I have always emphasized the need for its being placed on a planned and selective basis. The present method is only creating a difficult unemployment problem in addition to that which already exists.
As it has been discussed so extensively already, I do not intend to speak further of the disaster which has struck the farmers of this country and which is referred to briefly in the speech from the throne. I will only mention the seriousness of the impact upon our whole economy of the dreadful foot-and-mouth disease which is now epidemic in one area of Canada, and I will seek to emphasize its importance to our export trade.
Our exports to the United States have been very high. Now an important part of that export trade is threatened. A very important part of that export trade has been completely stopped for the time being. At the same time we appear to be in danger of losing our historic British markets. In spite of the seriousness of the situation there is in the speech from the throne no suggestion that anything effective is being done to find some way to continue that vitally important export trade to the British isles. The extent of the threat to agriculture generally can be illustrated by the fact that we have been selling large quantities of cheese to Britain for nearly one hundred years. It has been our main market for this very important industry which is vital to the dairy industry of this country. So far this year, so far as I have been able to ascertain, no orders from Bri-55704-11J
The Address-Mr. Drew
tain have yet been placed for cheese, and doubt has been expressed that the British will be able to buy our cheese. This would be an extremely serious blow to the dairy industry in Canada on top of the grave and serious blow it has received from another source and from which it is now suffering. This is merely another example of the dangers confronting all branches of agriculture because of the failure of the government to retain our British markets.
I have touched on matters that are causing great concern to the people of Canada at this time. These things that I have mentioned were some of the things in regard to which the people of this country have been demanding action. Instead of meeting those demands, this government has taxed scores of thousands of Canadians out of employment. It has taxed many of our industries into stagnation. Its overtaxation has been a compound of fraud and futility. It has directly increased inflation in many ways to which I have already referred.
May I remind this government and the members of this house that while this was being done, religious, labour, agricultural, social, commercial, manufacturing, mining and other well-recognized organizations across Canada were asking in the clearest and most expressive terms for relief from the crushing load of unnecessary taxation. Instead of dealing with any of these urgent problems the government made a great show of giving Canada some new status of maturity.
To many Canadians this all seemed1 very strange. They thought Canada had grown up long ago. Many Canadians were not aware that we needed any evidence that we had grown up. Many Canadians remembered their own history. They remembered that Sir John Macdonald had introduced a national policy which asserted, without any reservation, Canada's complete sovereignty and Canada's unchallengeable right to protect its own interests, even if that meant the disadvantage of the people of Great Britain, the United States, or any other country in the world. Long before the turn of this century, Sir John Macdonald said that, whatever sympathy and affection he might have for the people of Britain, his first concern was not for the unemployed of another country but for the unemployed here in Canada. In that declaration he asserted his belief, which was the accepted one, that Canada was a nation of full maturity with full sovereignty over its own affairs. Other Canadians remembered that the status of the dominions defined in the Statute of Westminster was not drafted or devised at that time, but was merely a restatement, in statutory form, of the Balfour

The Address-Mr. Drew declaration, years before. Word by word it followed that definition of the equality of the nations within the commonwealth which had been found necessary because of Sir Robert Borden's insistence that Canada sign the treaty of Versailles in 1919 as a nation sovereign in every respect.
There were many others who remembered that the pomp and circumstance of the Department of External Affairs which we see today was no newly discovered expression of Canada's place in international affairs but that it was also Sir Robert Borden who initiated the policy of diplomatic representation at Washington which began our formal representation outside of Canada throughout the world.
Many Canadians were under the impression that we had grown up to reasonably advanced maturity when, of our own free will, Canada made its own declaration of war on Germany in 1914 in order to protect the freedom of the Canada we knew.
To many Canadians who thought we had grown up long ago and .to whom it never occurred: that any steps were necessary to define or to declare our national maturity, it seems possible that some of the things that have been happening were for other reasons than those which were explained at the time. They have been asking if it is possible that it was done to divert attention from as grave and difficult problems as any that have ever confronted this nation.
In any event much time and effort were devoted to matters in regard to which there has been no evidence before this house of any extensive demand, while at the same time the government ignored the widespread and urgent request that something be done in regard to the high cost of living, inflation, overtaxation, employment and the assurance of continued export markets. Not for the first time in history people were offered shows and banners to divert their attention from their immediate and urgent needs.
It makes no difference what the intention was. We all know what impression has been created in the minds of a very large number of our people. No matter how much any one of us might feel that it was desirable not to bring this subject forward for discussion at this time, it is not possible to ignore the resolutions forwarded to the government, copies of which have come to me and have been sent to other members of parliament, and also the very large numbers of letters from every part of Canada expressing the fear that Canada's ties with the crown and the commonwealth have been weakened by some of these events.
May I emphasize the fact that I am simply referring to opinions which have been expressed by responsible organizations as well as individuals. Members of parliament cannot disregard those opinions, whether any member of the government or of this house may think that they are right or wrong. May I point out that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) recognized the fact that this concern was in the minds of many of our people. He indicated that, in his opinion, it had reached the point and had reached proportions which called for a statement from him. It was obviously for that reason that he discussed these matters at a press conference on January 25 last. Some of the subjects to which reference was made at that time are now by tradition and the rules of parliament no longer subjects for discussion here. I trust that our traditions and our rules will be respected in this regard.
One subject which the Prime Minister did discuss, however, on January 25 can and should be discussed and does afford a very clear example of the kind of uncertainty which is bringing uneasy thoughts to the minds of many of our people in every part of Canada. The Prime Minister, members of the government, and in fact I am sure all the members of this house are well aware of that uneasiness which they have seen expressed in the resolutions and letters which they have received.
I refer particularly to the confusion and uncertainty surrounding the word "dominion". At the press conference to which I have referred, the Prime Minister had this to say:
We are a dominion and there is nothing I or the government or parliament can do about it so long as the British North America Act is in force. Canada is a dominion and Ottawa is a city. We do not always refer to it as the city of Ottawa and the imperial conferences' documents refer to this country as Canada.
He also made this very positive statement:
The government does not deny, nor have we any desire to deny, that Canada is one of the king's dominions.
Just as the Prime Minister thought it necessary to deal with this subject on January 25, because of the uneasiness which had been expressed, and which he expressed, so also I believe it is my duty to refer to it today at the first opportunity which presents itself to discuss the subject in this house during the present session.
I do not see how it would be possible for anyone who recognizes our constitution for what it is to disagree with the words of the Prime Minister which I have quoted. Nevertheless, something has been happening which

has made people uneasy and in some way changes have occurred in the use of the word "dominion" which have resulted in an apparent attempt to lessen its use. Now some new confusion has been caused by the use of the word "realm". The word was used in the proclamation of the accession to the throne of our new queen as a word which would embrace the nations and territories within the commonwealth. They include the United Kingdom, the dominions, the Commonwealth of Australia, the Republic of India and all the other territories under other names which give allegiance to the crown.
There was no suggestion that this proclamation substituted the word "realm" for such varied descriptive names as United Kingdom, commonwealth, republic or dominion. They all continue to bear the description given to them in their own constitutions.
Our constitution still describes our federated nation as a dominion under the name of Canada. To every Canadian who respects the constitution that must remain the name unless it is changed by such procedure as is provided in the constitution itself. That act has not been amended. Therefore, the question before us is not whether the word "dominion" or "realm" or any other word is preferable in referring to Canada. Other names have been suggested, as other names were suggested both at Charlottetown and Quebec before confederation. We all know that Sir John Macdonald wanted this nation to be described as "the kingdom of Canada". That suggestion was not accepted. The unanimous decision was to call Canada a "dominion" and the word "dominion" is still embedded in our constitution, as the Prime Minister has so correctly emphasized.
The question therefore is not the desirability of one name or another. The question that each one of us must consider is whether this government has any authority to do anything to substitute in government documents, communications of any kind, or anywhere else, another word for any word contained in the existing constitution, without the consent, not only of this parliament, but of the provinces, which have a very great interest in the constitution under which they carry on their affairs.
If the principle be accepted that the government has the authority to change the use of one word, it would have equal authority to change the use of any other word, with all the consequences that would flow from the change and the use of that other word as well. That is something which should be remembered by everyone who regards that constitution as a document of the utmost importance to all Canadians.
The Address-Mr. Drew
No matter how innocent of any attempt to destroy the sanctity of the constitution the government may be, the opinion that the government has been tampering with the constitution has been expressed in too many resolutions and by too many individuals throughout the past few months to leave any doubt that large numbers of Canadians, whatever those numbers may be, have reached the conclusion that the government in this case had adopted the attitude which was expressed on another occasion to which I have already referred, when the house was told by one of the senior members of the government "If we wanted to get away with it, who is going to stop us?"
May I repeat that the statement made by the Prime Minister on January 25, which I have already quoted, would seem to answer this uncertainty which has been expressed by so many of our people, but the uneasiness still persists, as is known to the government and other hon. members, and it has been strengthened by the fact that no matter what explanation may be given of the constitutional position, it has been a matter of general and public comment that in statements and public documents issued by the government the word is being used less and less. In fact this has been so noticeable that at least one magazine with a very large circulation in this country which has been in the habit of reviewing Canadian events under the heading of the word "dominion" has now substituted the word "realm".
This is not a healthy state of affairs. The very fact that we are told on the one hand that Canada is a dominion and that there is nothing that the Prime Minister, the government or parliament can do about it until there is an amendment to the British North America Act, while at the same time things are being done which leave the impression that the name is being discarded, produces an atmosphere of uncertainty, confusion and frustration, which could have very unhappy consequences.
One of the difficulties in trying to remove the uncertainty which exists is that the Prime Minister has left the impression on other occasions that he did favour the dropping of this name because of the sincere belief by many loyal Canadians in all parts of Canada that the word "dominion" implied dependence or submission. The Prime Minister also pointed out that there were those who regarded the word as having the very opposite meaning in its application to Canada and that it conveyed the impression of complete authority and sovereignty over our own affairs.

The Address-Mr. Drew
There is no doubt that this difference of opinion does exist and that both views are held and have been expressed by men and women whose loyalty to the crown, the commonwealth and Canada cannot be questioned in any way. The question, however, which I believe to be far more important than the definition or use of the word is the constitutional effect of any attempt by this government to change or diminish in any way the effect of a single word or sentence in the British North America Act, which is our basic constitution. No matter what point of view may be held about the use of the word "dominion", respect for the integrity of the constitution is something in regard to which all Canadians should be in agreement if they understand the possible consequences of accepting the proposition that this or any other government could have the right to usurp the power to change the constitution in whole or in part.
So that we may consider this from the strictly constitutional point of view and the importance of this subject to those who regard our constitution as the sacred charter of the rights of the people who live in the ten provinces of this vast nation of ours, I propose to read the opening sections of the British North America Act, as now amended and as they now stand in the statute, so that we may all recall the manner in which the name came to be used:
Whereas the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have expressed their desire to he federally united into one dominion under the crown of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, with a constitution similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom:
And whereas such a union would conduce to the welfare of the provinces and promote the interests of the British empire:
And whereas on the establishment of the union by authority of parliament it is expedient, not only that the constitution of the legislative authority in the dominion be provided for, but also that the nature of the executive government therein be declared:
And whereas it is expedient that provision be made for the eventual admission into the union of other parts of British North America:
I.	Preliminary
1.	This act may be cited as the British North America Act, 1867.
2.	Repealed.
3.	It shall be lawful for the queen, by and with the advice of Her Majesty's most honourable privy council, to declare by proclamation that, on and' after a day therein appointed, not being more than six months after the passing of this act, the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick shall form and be one dominion under the name of Canada; and on and after that day those three provinces shall form and be one dominion under that name accordingly.
After these opening declarations come the operative sections defining the legislative and
executive powers, the setting up of the Senate and the House of Commons, the constitution of provincial legislatures, the reservation of special provincial rights, and so on. That was and is our basic constitution. Some insist that it was a pact. Some contend that it was merely a statute and should be placed at no higher level. Whatever it may be called, the fact remains that it was a statutory interpretation of a solemn agreement, arrived at by the consent of the representatives of the four original provinces, with the authority and approval of the people whom they represented. Without agreement as to the details of the British North America Act there would have been no Canada as we know it today.
It was only upon the basis of that solemn covenant that this nation now embracing all the territory north of the United States from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and to the Arctic ocean on the north, is united under the single name of Canada.
Unless it had been understood that this statute could only be amended by the decision of the parliament of Canada and the provinces where their common interests were affected, then there would have been no agreement at all because those who cherished ancient rights, customs and laws in the different provinces looked to that constitution as the firm guarantee of those rights, no matter what government might be in power in the future.
The wording represented a meeting of minds of the representatives of the two great races which joined to form one united Canada. That part of the British North America Act which I have quoted recites the fact that the provinces, through their representatives, had expressed their desire -and it was their unanimous desire-to be federally united into one dominion under the crown. The words and form of the statute were approved by the representatives of the provinces before it became law. It will be recalled that revisions were made even after the earlier drafts to meet the opinions of those representatives of what was to be Canada who were then in London. There were differences of opinion in regard to some of the words and some of the provisions. As I have already recalled, Sir John Macdonald preferred the word "kingdom" to the name "dominion". He also wanted a greater centralization of authority than was finally agreed upon.
Those differences in detail and principle were resolved by responsible and earnest men, anxious to ensure the unity of this great

experiment of Canada, one of the most exhilarating and hopeful experiments that men have ever made. Under that constitution, representing concessions and agreement so that cherished rights might be preserved and precious local traditions protected, that act became the charter of our own particular form of democracy. As responsible representatives of the people of Canada it is our duty today to remember the manner in which this constitution came into being and our obligation not to disturb it in whole or in part, unless and until this parliament and the provincial legislatures shall have agreed as to the manner in which it shall be changed.
The Prime Minister has caused some concern and uncertainty by statements he made in this house. In referring to the act he said:
It is drawn to describe this country not as the dominion of Canada but as a dominion under the name of Canada. For us that name is sufficient.
There are those who find it difficult to understand this fine distinction. If we are a dominion under the name of Canada, they still are of the opinion that it does not seem inaccurate to describe ourselves as the "Dominion of Canada", and have so expressed themselves. I do not wish to treat this very solemn subject lightly, but I must confess that the distinction drawn by the Prime Minister does seem a little like that put forward by Tweedledee in "Alice in Wonderland" when he said:
Contrariwise if it was so, it might be: and if it were so, it would be; but as it isn't it ain't. That's logic.
Unfortunately, there are those, and they may be many, who are unable to see the logic of this contention.
Whatever the logic may be, however, my point is simply this. This, above any other time, is not a time to achieve by indirection anything that should be done by direct and open methods here in this parliament. This is not a time to leave any uncertainty in the minds of our people as to the designation and the constitutional position of this nation of which we are all so proud, and I emphasize the word "all". We all love the name of Canada. No country in the whole world has brighter prospects than those which open out before our eyes. But like every other country the very existence of Canada as a nation depends upon a constitution which defines the kind of nation that it is. If in the opinion of any of our people the names used, the distribution of power, the reservation of rights, or any other detail in that constitution may not be satisfactory, changes can be made by consent of the people through their representatives in the parliament of
The Address-Mr. Drew Canada and the legislatures of the ten provinces. But let there be no change, directly or indirectly, by the usurpation of unconstitutional authority by this or any other government.
If changes are desired, then in a spirit of good will, as responsible and reasonable human beings, recognizing that we are not here as individuals but simply as representatives and servants of the people, let us discuss what those changes should be. In that way and in that way alone should anything in our constitution be amended, either formally, or by the expressed wish of this or any succeeding parliament. The very fact that in the opening sections of the British North America Act which I have quoted there is one section which has been repealed strengthens the very point that I am making. The fact that appropriate steps were taken by constitutional means to repeal section 2 while the other words that I have read remained unchanged emphasizes the fact that it was not the intention of this parliament, at any time that this subject was before them for discussion, to change the word or form of that act except to the extent that the words and form have already been changed.
I have discussed this subject because not one of us can be unaware that many people's minds are greatly disturbed. We need not attempt to reach any arithmetical calculation as to how many people have expressed their uneasiness about this situation. The Prime Minister recognized that it had reached sufficient proportions that it was desirable for him to discuss the matter at a press conference which would carry his opinion and statements to the people of Canada. That is the reason I am discussing this subject here today.
At a time when this country stands before the whole world as a bright and shining example of the way in which people of different races and tradition can unite in harmony and good will, there is a solemn duty upon each one of us to do nothing that will disturb in any way the basis of that unity and understanding. As the Prime Minister has said, the law stands unchanged. That being so, I have no intention of dividing the house on this question. On the contrary, I hope that with the uncertainties that must be recognized we can all agree without any reservation that no doubt will be left in the mind of any Canadian that if there are to be changes we can discuss any proposal for any change which may be brought before this house in a sensible, orderly and friendly manner.

The Address-Mr. Drew
Whatever legal or other terminology we apply to the British North America Act, whether we call it a pact or call it something else, it was in fact a solemn agreement entered into by our provinces, ordained and established by their people, which brought into being this nation which now stands strong and united before the whole world.
It must follow that no change should or can be made in our constitution, not a word of it changed, not a principle or provision or implication of it altered, without consultation with or agreement by the representatives of the people themselves in this parliament and in the legislatures of the ten provinces.
It is their property, their protection, their safeguard, the ark of the covenant of their liberties and rights; ana no group of men, no single government, possesses the right, or ever could possess the right, to alter a word or a syllable in it which in any way or in the remotest manner might affect its guarantees, its safeguards or its principles. Here, in truth, we can say with Junius that when the constitution is invaded, when the first original right of the people, from which all laws derive their authority, is directly or indirectly attacked, then no right is safe for anybody. It is with that thought in mind and with great pride in the unity which has been achieved under our own constitution that I do so earnestly hope that, no matter what other differences of opinion may divide us from time to time, every member of this house will be of one mind in guarding this charter of our freedom.
This solemn declaration of unity, under which so many millions of Canadians have lived in harmony, peace and increasing security, tells us that this great and sovereign nation which bears the proud name of Canada is today a dominion within that world-wide fellowship of free men and women who express their common loyalty to Her Gracious Majesty, Queen Elizabeth II. Such at this time is the constitutional style and title of the great and beloved country that, with unswerving loyalty and fidelity, each one of us here is solemnly sworn to serve.
I move, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon):
That the following he added to the address:
"We regret that Your Excellency's advisers:
(a)	continue to impose excessive, burdensome and unjust taxation;
(b)	refuse to eliminate waste and extravagance and to cut down the cost of government;
(c)	fail to take adequate steps to deal effectively with inflation and the high cost of living."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure

for me to join the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) in extending congratulations to the mover (Mr. George) and the seconder (Mr. Gauthier, Lake St. John) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The hon. member for Westmorland and the hon. member for Lake St. John are among the newer members of the house, having entered parliament for the first time after the general election of 1949, but I believe we can all say to them that as their colleagues we are proud of the manner in which they acquitted themselves in the performance of what the leader of the opposition has referred to as a task imposed upon them. It has been my privilege for some sessions now to invite hon. members of the house to move and second the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and each time I have found that their reaction has not been that I was imposing a task upon them, but that I was extending to them a privilege which they were very glad to accept, and which in the years I have been here I think all members will agree they have performed in a manner that was a credit both to them and to the constituencies they represent in the house.
I am sure we agree with the leader of the opposition that the two hon. gentlemen to whom I have referred did credit to themselves and to their constituencies. They both spoke of the history of the regions they represent, of the natural resources of those regions, and of the industrial development that has recently taken place there. I also agree with the leader of the opposition that, though all of us may not accept their assertion that those two regions are among the most favoured in Canada, we all accept their assertion that they are very delightful places for human beings to inhabit. They spoke of the industrial developments of those regions in, I thought, a rather modest vein. They said they were referring to them because they realized they were typical of what was happening throughout the whole extent of this land from one ocean to the other.
I also wish to extend congratulations to the leader of the opposition for having communicated to us a very carefully prepared speech in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I am not going to deal with all that was contained in his speech, and I must confess to you, Mr. Speaker, that I have not come here with any notes, and have only those I made during the course of the interesting discourse to which we have just listened.
Perhaps because it is rather fresher in our memories than other parts of the hon. gentleman's speech I might refer at once

The Address-Mr. St. Laurent
to the statement he has made, and even repeated three or four times, that I recognized that there was uneasiness among some of our Canadian fellow citizens about the use of the word "dominion", and that if I had not recognized that I would not have mentioned it at a press conference which took place on the 25th of January. I am sure the leader of the opposition has had press conferences himself, and I think he realizes as well as I do that the questions dealt with at these press conferences are those that are suggested by the newspapermen who are there. They ask the questions, and it was in response to questions that were being put to me about this matter that I made the statements to which he refers.
I do not think it requires any long discourse to assure everyone in Canada that neither the government nor even parliament can change one iota of our constitution except as the constitution provides. If any changes have to be made they will have to be made in the constitutional way, and that constitutional way may not always be the way in which section 2 of the British North America Act was repealed. It was repealed merely in the process of the revision of the British statutes without any reference to the Canadian authorities at all. It was dropped because it was felt it was unnecessary. The publications we have containing the text of the statute also contain notes prepared by the law officers who edited these editions.
With respect to section 2 the note is:
Section 2 was repealed by the Statute Law Revision Act of 1893 (chapter 14).
Some of the repeals or changes that have been made by the statute revision acts have caused some uncertainty and embarrassment, and I understand from the law officers that after correspondence in that regard those who now prepare consolidations or revisions of the statute are more careful and do communicate with Canada about anything that is to be done to the British North America Act.
But that does not mean no change has in fact taken place since confederation. The Canadian nation has not stood still since 1867; and there is no doubt that without any change in the terms of the constitution, the position of Canada, and of the other dominions described as such in the Statute of Westminster, is recognized to be different now from what it was in 1867. While there will never be any attempt by this government, as long as I am a member of it, to have any change made by the government itself in the constitution, from time to time,
when proper occasion arises, it may be suggested that parliament make some changes in some statutes where "Dominion of Canada" is used as the name of the country, which under the constitution is simply Canada. That is all there is about that matter.
No doubt there will also be some change in the language each of us uses to express his concept of the position this nation now occupies in the commonwealth of British nations. In that regard the hon. gentleman referred to the use of the word "realm" in the proclamation that was issued in the United Kingdom on February 6 following the lamented death of our beloved sovereign George VI. I have the proclamation here. As I read it I did not take it that "realm" was intended to include the Republic of India, but that the inclusion of India was intended to be achieved by the use of the words "head of the commonwealth". We had no previous information about the description found there, with respect to which I may say here, so that there may be no doubt about it, I had no discussion whatever with the Right Hon. Winston Churchill while he was here. The only reference was that made in a jocular way during the course of his speech at the dinner given him at the Chateau Laurier, and that I understood was good fun, as a part of his speech, when he referred to his habit of using the word "dominion". I was quite surprised to find this description in the proclamation, but even if we had been given notice of it we would not have dared to use it ourselves in our proclamation, because we would have felt that it would not have been proper for us to presume to make any change in what is the legal royal style and title of the sovereign. That proclamation reads as follows:
Whereas it hath pleased Almighty God to call to His Mercy our late Sovereign Lord King George the Sixth of Blessed and Glorious Memory by whose Decease the Crown is solely and rightfully come to the High and Mighty Princess Elizabeth Alexandra Mary: We, therefore, the Lords Spiritual and Temporal of this Realm, being here assisted with these of His late Majesty's Privy Council, with representatives of other members of the Commonwealth, with other Principal Gentlemen of Quality, with the Lord Mayor, Aldermen and Citizens of London, do now hereby with one voice and Consent of Tongue and Heart publish and proclaim that the High and Mighty Princess Elizabeth Alexandra Mary is now, by the Death of our late Sovereign of Happy Memory, become Queen Elizabeth the Second, by the Grace of God Queen of this Realm and of all Her other Realms and Territories, Head of the Commonwealth, Defender of the Faith . . .
When I read this I felt quite convinced that it was not intended to imply that India was one of the other realms and territories
170

The Address-Mr. St. Laurent of our gracious sovereign, but that, notwithstanding the fact that India had become a republic, the people of that republic still recognized the sovereign of the commonwealth as the head of the commonwealth.
I am sure we all agree with one statement of the leader of the opposition. Oh, there may be a few individual exceptions, but so few as not to be of serious import in that connection. We all agree in our firm loyalty to our monarchical institutions, of which our gracious Queen Elizabeth II is now the head and sovereign. That loyalty is all the more widespread and universal in this country because it is felt that it implies no acceptance of any secondary position, but an acceptance of the position recognized in Lord Balfour's declaration for which, with the leader of the opposition, I am quite prepared to give great credit to the late Sir Robert Borden who at an earlier time, as prime minister of Canada, was contending for the right of this country to sign the treaty of Versailles as a nation. I was saying that the unquestioned loyalty to the sovereign, to the crown and to our monarchical institutions is all the more universal and firm and sincere because it is recognized that the queen's subjects in Canada are the equal of the queen's subjects in any of her realms all over the world.
There is no doubt that there is uneasiness in some quarters because they have felt there was some desire to weaken these links between the free peoples of the commonwealth of British nations. But there is also no doubt that there was some uneasiness among others in Canada who felt that there was resentment over the attainment by Canadian citizens of equality of status with Her Majesty's subjects in any of her realms all over the world. No doubt that will continue to be manifested; but today I think we had a pretty good example of how careful Canadians wish to be to avoid anything that may create controversy between them in that regard, in what was done by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Arsenault)-and I can assure you it was not suggested to him as far as I know-when he asked for leave to withdraw the bill he has had before the house on two or twree previous occasions to change the statutory name of the holiday provided for on July 1 in our statutes. I think the hon. member deserves to be congratulated because, in spite of his feeling that it would be preferable to change that name, he has decided not to press it at this time and not to occasion unnecessary disputes about matters with respect to which-again repeating the language used by the leader of the opposition-all Canadians, loyal in their 

attachment to the crown and to our institutions, have diverging views about which they feel quite strongly. I think we can leave it at that, Mr. Speaker, and that it would be the desire of all hon. members of the house to do as the leader of the opposition said was his intention, namely not to attempt to divide us on matters of that kind but to attempt to continue, to enlarge and to strengthen the unity of feeling and purpose among all Canadians in their devotion and attachment to their democratic institutions, under their monarchical form, and under the constitution which was written into the statute books in 1867.
The hon. member has welcomed the statement in the speech from the throne that there would be amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Veterans Benefit Act, but he has stated that the speech from the throne does not disclose what those amendments will do. I think the hon. gentleman will agree that it is not usual to set out in the speech from the throne the details of legislation. I feel convinced that the recommendation which will be brought before parliament in that regard will satisfy a large majority of the members of the house that fair proposals are being put before parliament in order to deal with the difficulty that quite large numbers of those who have served their country and their fellow citizens so well were experiencing under the scales of allowances that have heretofore been provided.
The leader of the opposition says that it is also a discouraging statement because it does not say what the amendments will be and furthermore because, as he puts it, it does not disclose that the government has any cure-all for the ills of the world at the present time. That is unfortunate but it is true. The government has no cure-all for the conditions prevailing in the world at the present time. It may be that that is a fair subject of criticism.
The hon. gentleman has said it was the duty of the opposition to co-operate with the government when it felt that the government was doing something constructive and which would be for the welfare of the community generally. I thank him for the degree to which that co-operation has been extended in past sessions and in the present one thus far. I have no quarrel with him for his suggestion that it is also the duty of the opposition, and even of all members of parliament, freely to express their minds about the propriety or impropriety of the administrative acts that it is the duty and responsibility of the government, under the constitution, to have carried out in the name

of the sovereign. We will endeavour to meet, as best we can-I will not promise that the record will be any better than it has been in the past-the criticism that may be levelled against us in that regard.
Then the leader of the opposition spoke about the high cost of living. May I say that we have been endeavouring to deal with the high cost of living, particularly since the outbreak of the Korean war, which, as the hon. gentleman has said, put a pressure upon prices, not only in this country but in all the free nations of the world. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that in the methods that we have adopted to combat that inflation we have been as fortunate-I will perhaps not say as wise-as any others anywhere in the world, although we have not been able to do as is suggested, namely devise anti-inflationary measures that would be sufficient to outbalance the inflationary pressures. What has happened here is what has happened everywhere else in the world. Again I am not boasting. It may be that it was our good fortune which was responsible, but our good fortune has been such that it has been favourably commented upon in the press of many other countries- a fact which perhaps is only another example of that human tendency to see the greener pastures farther away.
For the last couple of months there has not been anything startling in the cost-of-living index issued by the bureau of statistics, but there appears to be a trend that indicates a stabilization. This gives some Canadians the hope that the peak has been reached and that the measures which the hon. gentleman has described as over-severe have commenced to produce the salutary effect for which they were devised.
The leader of the opposition spoke about crushing taxation. Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) has been doing his best to collect the amount of taxes provided for by the rates of taxation fixed by this House of Commons. Had he not done so, he would have been derelict in his duty. It is not the government that imposes taxation. It is the government that recommends to parliament what the rates will be; but it was parliament itself that, in the last budget, voted the rates of taxation that had to be applied to the Canadian taxpayers.

The word "conservative", you know, is like the word "dominion". There are occasions when it can be properly used.
There is no doubt that this thing which is described under the initials "G.N.P." is quite considerably larger than was forecast by the Minister of Finance last year. My own rough estimate is that that substantial increase is going to mean something not far from $300 million more revenue than was forecast on a smaller "G.N.P." That may be embarrassing for the Minister of Finance and those who helped him make his forecast, and it may entitle some to say:	"Well, you
are not a very good prophet"; but I think it is very fortunate for the Canadian people that their economy was that much more buoyant than had been forecast.
Then there was expected to be obtained from United States sources for the purpose of our rearmament probably not less than $200 million worth of equipment for which orders have been placed, and which will not be delivered, though it was expected to be delivered in the fiscal year 1951-1952, and will not therefore be paid for out of the expenditure of 1951-52. That again may be somewhat embarrassing for the Minister of National Defence. He had, I know, entered the fiscal period with grave doubts as to whether he would have enough in his appropriations to pay for what he was going to get

during the year; but he did not get it as fast as he hoped he would, and it has not had to be paid for, and that accounts for a substantial portion of what is called this overtaxation. I do not think there is anything more I can usefully say with respect to that matter. I repeat, embarrassing as it may be for the government, for those who made the forecast, it is very fortunate for the Canadian people that it happened. Had it gone to the same extent in the other direction it would have been most unfortunate also for the government and also for the Canadian people.
There is the suggestion that taxation has been inflationary. I think the hon. gentleman said that something of the order of $250 per family of five had been taken away from Canadians, which they themselves would have had available to spend had it not thus been taken. Well, I am not an economist, but I have always understood that the pressure on prices resulted from the disproportion between the purchasing power that was available and the amount of commodities that were there to be purchased. And if the amount of commodities had remained what it was, and there had been $250 more purchasing power for every family of five- well, in my simple logic I would come to the conclusion that that would have added to the inflationary pressure instead of the fact of its having been withdrawn as purchasing power adding to the inflationary pressure.
