Well, the hon. member may be much wiser than I am in these matters, but I am not convinced by his interruptions that my reasoning is wrong. It is perhaps unfortunate that I am so thickheaded, but it happens to be so.
There is no doubt that we all deplore the fact that we have not here in this country, under present conditions where we have to take so much for rearmament, devised antiinflationary measures which would outbalance the inflationary pressure that has not been possible either in any other country of the world. We have not been able to do it, and I do not think we are going to be able to do it in the future. I think we just have to cope with those inflationary pressures as best we can, and keep them within bounds, to the extent to which that is possible.
I do not think this can be done by control measures. I think you have got to do it-if you are going to have any lasting results- by attacking the evil at its source. Hon. members I am sure would agree with that. The most effective way would be to make more commodities available to be exchanged for the purchasing power distributed-and distributed so widely-among the public. I

think everyone must agree that that is the only or, if not the only, certainly the surest way of combating effectively and of retarding inflation.
The hon. member says that there has never been any argument submitted by him or by those whom he leads in the house against the propriety of credit restrictions, but he says that our credit restrictions have been excessive. They were devised to serve a purpose which to a certain extent is recognized. I am not sure whether it is in Mr. Muir's address, but it certainly is in the address of the president of the Bank of Toronto, and certainly is in the address of the president of the Bank of Montreal. Those measures have been, to a certain extent, effective, and they have served the purposes for which they were devised.
I have been seeing for the last three or four days full-page advertisements addressed to Mr. St. Laurent telling him that it is very unfortunate that there are taxes on washing machines. I think it is unfortunate that there are taxes on washing machines. It is unfortunate that there are-well, as a matter of fact, it is unfortunate that there is any taxation at all. But no taxation is an ideal which it is not possible to achieve under conditions of human society as organized in our day.
The hon. member said that he hoped there would be a commitment by the Prime Minister this afternoon to remove this crushing burden of taxation placed on the Canadian people. Well, the Prime Minister can make no such commitment. There is no doubt that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and his advisers and colleagues will be looking at the whole picture and at each individual item; and it may very well be that there will be some adjustments. But so long as the world situation continues as it is, I cannot hold out any hope to the Canadian people of any substantial reduction in the scale of the rate of taxation in this country.
In spite of everything we try to do, all hon. members will bear witness to the fact that there are a great many things requested that are not done by the Canadian government, and that could not be done by the Canadian government with the present scale of taxation. I am sure we will hear during this session very earnest pleas for increases in several of the fields in which moneys raised by taxation are at present expended. We will nave to listen to them; we will have to give them careful consideration. But we will also have to bear in mind the fact that the government does not print money: The government taxes money out of the pockets of the Canadian taxpayers. And I think that most
The Address-Mr. St. Laurent Canadian taxpayers feel that under semipeaceful conditions, even under conditions of a cold war, taxation has just about reached as high limits as it is proper for the people to bear at the present time.
The hon. member said he would ask to have set up at an early date the committee on defence expenditures. I am sure he will have noticed that I have given notice to have that committee set up, and I shall bring on the notice just as soon as it seems convenient to do so; because I think it is quite proper that this committee should scrutinize the expenditures that are being made for defence purposes. I feel sure that the Canadian people want to be assured that these huge sums- because they are huge sums-are being properly expended, and that they are not being called upon year after year to bear this heavy burden of taxation only to be confronted with a failure to make proper provision for our share of this joint effort to preserve peace in the world, and to make it unlikely that aggression against us could be successful.
The hon. member has spoken about unemployment. There are certain regions where unemployment has developed. Possibly no region has been more seriously affected than the city of Toronto, and the surrounding area. There is no region to which people have flocked since defence production orders have commenced to be placed in greater numbers than they have to the Toronto area, because it so happens that there were more of these so-called war industries located there than there were elsewhere.
There is unemployment. I think it is seasonal unemployment. It is somewhat larger than it was in 1951. It is not as large as it was in 1950. And there are more employed at the present time than were ever employed before. It will be recalled that there was serious anxiety in 1950 about the situation. There was a pretty widespread feeling that the government should embark upon a plan of public construction to mop up the unemployment. Well, within months the manpower supply in Canada was being taxed to the very limits.
The hon. member has suggested that the number of immigrants who have entered Canada has added to the unemployment problem. The number of immigrants who happen to be unemployed or not to have been placed is a very small percentage of those who have come in. It may be that if others had not come in and taken jobs we would not have as many employed in Canada at the present time as we now have.
It is not an easy problem at all times to balance exactly these equations where the
174	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. St. Laurent human factor is of such great importance. Generally speaking, I think the Canadian public were glad to see the extent to which there was immigration to this country in 1951. Though there may be a small percentage who have not been absorbed in the Canadian population, I feel confident that that will be cured within weeks and that the over-all result will be beneficial to the Canadian nation.
These matters have to be under constant scrutiny. I can assure the house, that, as far as this government is concerned, they are kept under constant scrutiny. In spite of the suggestion in one of the leading newspapers this morning which rather shocked me, the government does recognize its responsibility to this House of Commons and the Canadian people. I can give you the assurance that as far as each one of my colleagues and myself are concerned we do not shirk any part of our work, and we do plenty of it. We realize that we are trustees for the Canadian people through their representatives here in this house of parliament. None of us wants to remain on the job unless he is doing it in a manner which satisfies his conscience that he is not lagging.
That is the only assertion that I can make about the results of what we may hope to be able to do in the future. We have not a cure-all for the ills of the present day, but we are going to attend to them as efficiently and as assiduously as possible. We are going to recommend to parliament every measure in which we can feel any confidence as to its likelihood to make for the general welfare of the Canadian public.
The hon. gentleman said that he did not want to deal with the difficulties arising out of the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in a certain section of Saskatchewan. I suppose I am naturally inclined to be an optimist. I will confess that I derive some considerable satisfaction out of the fact that this is March 6 and there has been no further case found since February 19. That does raise one's hopes. I hope they will not be false hopes. I hope they will not be dashed.
The first thing that had to be attended to was the use of every means available to human ingenuity to eradicate this disease. Then means had to be taken to take care of those who had been particularly hit by the consequences of the disease. That is being done. I think there should be a most careful investigation of the officials who had to handle the situation which arose in and around Regina.
I still have confidence in the competence and efficiency of the gentlemen in the health of animals branch of the Department of


Agriculture. I think it would be only fair to them and to the public to have them come before a committee and be examined as to what they did, when they did it, why they did it and why they did not do something else. They occupy responsible positions. Should it be found that through lack either of knowledge or of diligence there was laxity, that should be brought to light and dealt with.
So far I think it would be wrong to the public and to them to prejudge until there has been this opportunity for them to make their full statements before this committee. I hope the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth (Mr. Charlton) will be there. I was most interested in hearing him discuss this malady in the house. I hope he will be there in the committee to see that every angle of what should or could have been done is properly investigated. I hope it will be shown that the confidence we all have, the confidence which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) expressed in his first words when he spoke in this house on this problem on Monday last, will prove not to have been misplaced.
In general I think the civil service of Canada is performing an efficient and conscientious job of work for the Canadian people. It happens sometimes that someone does make a mistake or someone does show some laxity. Fortunately for the Canadian public those occasions have been quite rare. I hope they will continue to be rare. I hope that the confidence the government, parliament and the Canadian people have, and have had for years, in the competence, honesty and diligence of the civil service of Canada will continue to be justified.
The hon. gentleman spoke of, and I wish to leave this to the last, the loss of the British markets to Canadian agriculture. That is unfortunate. I do not know what the history books will have to say about the conduct of the people of the British isles during the two world wars, but it would seem to us of this generation that they literally stripped themselves of their resources in the fight for freedom in those two wars. Unfortunately they have to import large quantities of their foodstuffs. In the past they were able to do this out of the income of their investments abroad and out of their exports to foreign markets.
Having made the sacrifices they made during the world wars they had very little investment abroad left to bear income. It so happened that industries had been developed in other parts of the world which made it more difficult for them to export their products to those markets. North America, Canada included, has not been unmindful of the consequences of the

sacrifices made for freedom by that great country. During the war this small country made very substantial contributions which, although voted in money, were realized in kind, in things produced here and exported to them. After the war we continued to do likewise. The hon. gentleman will remember that a loan of a billion and a quarter dollars was made at the time the loan of three and three-quarter billion dollars was made by the United States.
It so happens, however, that the forecasts of that time were not realized. The United Kingdom felt that it was in honour bound to make unrequited exports to countries in which sterling debts had been incurred as part of the war effort, and they just have not the dollars that would be required to continue to purchase supplies from Canadian producers that they can in any way at all get along without. It is unfortunate. I think that under present conditions in this country it would be difficult for us to provide, by way of either gift or loan, additional sums to pay for Canadian produce that was exported and was not paid for by the importers. Our trade last year is going to show an over-all deficit in our balance of payments made up only by the capital investments from the United States which have taken place in the course of the year 1951.
There again is a situation in which the one partial remedy would be the additional absorption of British exports, or, from our point of view, British imports, in the Canadian market. We have had complaints from more than one quarter that some of our unemployment was the consequence of competition by imports from the British market that could not be met by our Canadian industries. That is also something that has to be taken into account. We have to look at the repercussions of these things on every segment of the Canadian economy. Can we increase our absorption of exports from the United Kingdom to any substantial degree without disturbing our own economy?
The hon. gentleman said that three-quarters of a century ago Sir John A. Macdonald stated that, in spite of his love for and sympathy with the people of the British isles, if there were to be unemployment he would prefer to see unemployment there than to have unemployment produced in Canada. Human nature does not change very much. Whatever be the labels under which political parties go, the way in which they envisage the repercussions of their actions on those to whom they are responsible is pretty much the same. We have to take the same general view that Sir John A. Macdonald felt he had
The Address-Mr. St. Laurent to take of his duty, and our duty is to be more considerate of conditions in Canada than of conditions anywhere else in the world.
The only other way of recovering the British market would be by increasing, either in the form of mutual aid or in the form of loans, the number of dollars that the British treasury might expend. But it is not just dollars. They would have to take the equivalent of those dollars out of the annual production of the Canadian people, and) as long as we are going along consuming as we are consuming and investing in capital development as we have been investing we just have not got the possibility of balancing our own foreign, trade unless we get something for everything that we export. I am sorry that I am not an economist. Perhaps my task might be easier if I were. I am not sure that it would be. I think that the realistic situation is such that it requires more than the additional capacity I might have achieved from long studies of economics to deal with these problems in any other way than they are being dealt with by governments all over the world.
If we are not doing as good, a job as is being done elsewhere we should be condemned for not doing so, but if we are doing as well here as is being done elsewhere, though it may not be ideal and may not be as good as any of us would hope it could or should-be, I think we have to be realistic enough to realize that it is as good as can be done under existing circumstances.
In conclusion, I can tell the leader of the opposition and the house that we have not got anything up our sleeves, and that in the speech from the throne we did describe the legislative program that we intend to put before parliament during this session.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if my congratulations to the mover (Mr. George) and the seconder (Mr. Gauthier, Lake St. John) of the address are brief, they are nonetheless sincere. I join with others in the house in congratulating them. But, since my own time in the debate is limited, I do not propose to do more than to express to them my congratulations.
The speech from the throne, which very properly expressed sorrow at the passing of His late Majesty King George VI and expressed also our loyalty to Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, mentions a number of matters which will be brought before the house. It expresses concern regarding the international situation, and this concern is shared very deeply by most citizens of our country. And because I wish to devote some attention to this tonight, I am taking this opportunity of saying that any criticisms that I make of policy generally in regard to international matters will be made after very careful consideration. While I know that some misconstruction may be made of my remarks, nevertheless I think they are remarks someone should make regarding these matters.
This afternoon the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) referred to a recent statement that was issued by the national council of the C.C.F. I wish to say immediately that I was present when that statement was drafted, and that I approved of it. We have watched with a great deal of concern the recent developments in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Our statement says at the very outset that we continue to support the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, and
we support all the commitments that were made on behalf of Canada in this parliament in 1951.
The leader of the opposition said this afternoon that we were taking a position similar to that taken by Mr. Aneurin Bevan in the British House of Commons. That is not so. Mr. Bevan was criticizing and did criticize what was done in Britain in regard to expenditures last year on rearmament. Indeed, Mr. Churchill paid him the compliment not long ago of saying that Mr. Bevan had disagreed with what had been done from the wrong point of view, but nevertheless that he was right in the general criticisms he had made in 1951.
"We think that the policies of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization have fallen too completely under the military, to the exclusion of social and economic considerations in the maintenance or the building of western collective security. We believe that this emphasis has been unwise.
And not alone do we hold this view. I have before me the Times of London for February 26, a week ago last Tuesday, in which it refers to a statement that was issued following the Lisbon meeting of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. The heading of the editorial in this well-known conservative or independent paper is "The Phantom Army", and it says this:
It is difficult to understand either the meaning or the purpose of the communique published by the council of the North Atlantic treaty in Lisbon. This states in words which seem almost to have been chosen for their ambiguity-they have no other virtue-that the member nations will provide this year approximately fifty divisions in appropriate conditions of combat readiness.
Then it goes on to discuss the present situation in regard to the divisions that have already been set up, and: then points out that only about half that number have at present been established by the North Atlantic Treaty Organization nations. It goes on to say this:
Presumably the announcement was meant to impress someone, but it will not impress the Russians, who know very well the true state of affairs, and who have the sense to realize that any real plans for real divisions would be kept secret. Indeed this imaginative total with the still more imaginative promise of 85 or 100 divisions in two years' time seems to contain the maximum amount of provocation with the minimum amount of deterrent effect.
The leader of the opposition this afternoon said that in mentioning the fact that we thought that this had been promoted by representatives of the United States we were open to criticism. But the Times of London says this:
Even if it is meant only to impress the American congress, and the whole communique has a very American ring, it may fail in its object . . .

And so I say that the criticism we have made is one that is shared not only by socialists, democratic, and otherwise, but is shared by many Conservatives-and otherwise- throughout the world. As the house will remember, we have always emphasized article 2 of the North Atlantic treaty, which called for the integration of the economies of the participating nations in order to maintain the economic base upon which the security of western Europe must depend. The recent announcements from Lisbon, if attempted, we believe, will jeopardize the economic base upon which all else depends. And this afternoon when the leader of the opposition was speaking he urged the house to look very carefully into the economic obligations that we might undertake in- this parliament in regard to further expenditures on rearmament, and so on. I took down his words when he said, "We should inquire what would happen to our economy if we accepted any further commitments" for NATO.
So we have the leader of the opposition, not in the same words, but expressing to some extent the idea that we have tried to place before the house and country. And yesterday in the House of Commons in London Mr. Churchill indicated1 very clearly that. Great Britain had been unable to carry into effect the commitments the previous government had made in 1951. Indeed he was challenged in the house because he said they could not carry those commitments into effect. He said the rearmament program already assumed and authorized by the British parliament could not be carried out in the time allotted.
His words as reported in today's press were diese:
The rearmament program is much more likely to be carried out in four years than in three.
It is therefore difficult to understand the decisions taken at Lisbon to provide approximately fifty divisions in western Europe by the end of this year, when we are told that no more than twenty-five divisions exist now, and to provide ninety to one hundred divisions by the end of 1954 at a total cost of $300 billion. Translate those $300 billion into the budgets of all the NATO countries and see what results you get. I know that in our own country one of the ablest commentators on international affairs, Mr. J. B. McGeachy, of the Toronto Globe and Mail, speaking in the special news of the week commentary on Sunday evening, characterized the fifty divisions as a phantom army. As the London Times stated the Lisbon provisions for this phantom army contained "the maximum amount of provocation with the minimum deterrent effect".
The Address-Mr. Coldwell
It seems to us that Canada should take a realistic attitude and when necessary vigorously criticize, as in this instance the armament goal set at Lisbon because it is unrealistic. We of the C.C.F. believe that an attempt to carry out an excessive military program will cripple the possibilities for the economic rebuilding of Europe and other parts of the world and lead us into an entirely false sense of strength and security which indeed do not exist.
It seems to us that NATO has been influenced almost entirely by domestic and political considerations in the United States. This is an election year there. Most nations are dependent upon our great neighbour for financial and economic aid. Fortunately Canada has paid her own way and is in no sense dependent on the United States for financial or economic aid. Hence we are in a peculiar position of being able in NATO, and indeed in the United Nations when necessary, to give a lead towards the acceptance of more sensible and constructive policies than we have been getting. The Canadian government itself should be criticized for agreeing to policies which if carried through to a logical conclusion will we believe endanger the economic and social welfare of the world. I believe that that is exactly what the Kremlin wants and what the Kremlin is banking on, the collapse of the western European countries.
Let me say that the criticisms I have made of Canadian policy and United States leadership in no way imply unfriendliness towards the United States people, for whom I think we all have a high regard and respect. However, there are times when the friendship which exists between our two countries should enable us to speak candidly to one another.
There is one other thing I should like to say before I leave this point. I have not seen the evening news, but I doubt whether France has yet a government. As we all know, this is due to the economic situation in France. France cannot bear the additional burden that would be placed upon her if the Lisbon commitments were carried out fully. Consequently we are daring to say what many people in Canada, not only in our own party but in all other parties, are thinking and saying privately.
I should like to say something about Korea. I think there is deep disappointment with regard to the negotiations in Korea and the fact that we have failed to reach a ceasefire. There is no doubt that many people share the view expressed by the commander of the ground forces in Korea on March 12,

The Address-Mr. Coldwell 1951. According to the 1951 report of the Department of External Affairs, General Ridgway predicted that a military stalemate appeared probable and then he added, and I quote from page 12 of the report:
It would be a tremendous victory for the United Nations if the war ended1 with our forces in control up to the 3Sth parallel.
That is a statement made one year ago by General Ridgway as quoted by our own Department of External Affairs. Most people hoped when on November 27, 1951, an agreement was reached on the principles which should govern the definition of a cease-fire line, and such a line was then defined, that speedy agreement would be reached. When the North Korea aggression occurred in June, 1950, there was virtually unanimous support for United Nations action to prevent its success. There was a determination everywhere to drive the invading forces back beyond the 38th parallel, which the communist forces had passed.
That objective was achieved in October, 1950. What I am about to say, I say advisedly, because I remember being at the United Nations. It was then believed that the United Nations action would end on a defensive line at or near, probably just beyond, the 38th parallel. Those hopes were rudely shattered when General MacArthur unexpectedly launched an offensive toward the Yalu river and the Chinese border. The result was that the so-called Chinese volunteer forces entered the war in considerable force and a much more threatening situation immediately developed.
In February of 1951, I believe under United States leadership and perhaps pressure, the United Nations declared China to be an aggressor nation. Before voting for that declaration our own minister of external affairs declared it to be "premature and unwise". At the time we of this group described that vote as a mistake, and I think subsequent events have justified and confirmed that opinion. We hoped however that steps would be taken to end the war and certainly to prevent it developing into a new world war, which probably would be the outcome if war were taken into China.
We welcomed the opening of negotiations for a cease-fire and armistice about eight months ago. In common with people who have followed events, we have watched with growing misgivings the course of those negotiations. But we were hopeful, when the Chinese agreed on November 27 to a ceasefire line just north of the 38th parallel, a line which the United Nations troops would hold pending armistice negotiations, that other


matters in dispute would be settled and a cease-fire arrangement and subsequently peace attained.
We were doomed to disappointment because new considerations were constantly introduced by both sides. I am not blaming one side more than the other in this respect. In relation to the big issue of the armistice and peace the matters which have been introduced since the line was agreed upon appear to be minor in character. When the United Nations had achieved the original objective named last March by General Ridgway there should have been no insurmountable difficulty in ending this Korean war.
In our opinion the matters which have been introduced and which are now largely under discussion are political rather than military. We have held the opinion for some time-I stated this in Regina the first week in January-that the time has come when they should be the subject of what we might term political negotiations. It has been growing clearer all the time that the military leaders in Korea have reached a stalemate and that the time has arrived when governmental or political representatives of the nations actively engaged in the Korean war should assume responsibility for direct negotiations between the United Nations and the Chinese government at Peking to end the hostilities and secure an armistice prior to a peace settlement in Korea. I want to urge our government to take the initiative to this end. I do not believe that the intervention of the United Nations assembly or security council in the negotiations is possible or desirable on account of the kind of prolonged discussion that would develop in the assembly and because of the veto in the security council. Indeed, unfortunately the United Nations assembly is assuming more and more the character of a sounding board for Soviet propaganda and an instrument of international policy for the United States.
I believe that the suggestion we are making should be considered. I believe that a proposal should be made to the Peking government for negotiations among the nations whose troops, I repeat, are actively engaged in the Korean war. I think that proposal might be made by the United Kingdom; for let us remember that the United Kingdom recognizes the Peking government as the government of China. Whether or not such a proposal would be entertained and negotiations entered upon thereafter I do not know, but the attempt should be made, and again I say that I think Canada might suggest it to our allies in the Korean affair.

Many statements made by leading United States spokesmen have created a very uneasy feeling that a powerful group in that country not only is not anxious to achieve peace in the Far East but is determined to enlarge the war against China. Is there any evidence of that? I think there is quite a bit. Recently, for example, Mr. Foster Dulles appeared before the foreign relations committee of the United States senate when the Japanese treaty was under discussion, a treaty which he formulated and for which he secured support among the nations. Mr. Dulles therefore is an outstanding United States ambassador-at-large. Before that committee he declared that the United States must secure the removal of the present Peking government, and I am going to quote his exact words from the record. He said:
We cannot expect a change to take place automatically. To realize such a change will require something besides a negative and purely defensive policy in Asia on the part of the leaders of the free world, notably in the United States.
Taken in conjunction with the decision of the Japanese government to recognize the Chiang Kai-shek government on the island of Formosa as the government of China, which it is well known the British government did not wish to see done, the protests that have been made by the Burmese government against the activities and arming of nationalist Chinese troops in northern Burma, and the rearming of Japan, Mr. Dulles' statement indicates clearly that if we, the United Kingdom and other countries follow United States leadership in the Far East without making our own opinions known and adopting our own attitudes in this regard we are liable to be dragged into a disastrous adventure which will enable the communist dictators to achieve all their objectives. What I think our United States friends and neighbours are overlooking is that the Asian peoples have awakened and are determined to throw off the yoke of their ruling powers, both western imperialist and domestic, and I say nothing will prevent this.
Unfortunately except for the farsighted statesmanship of United Kingdom leaders in withdrawing from India, Pakistan and Burma, the granting of dominion status to Ceylon, and the recognition of Indonesian independence by the Netherlands, the support for reactionary leadership and imperial interests elsewhere in Asia, has, I believe, alienated from western influence vast masses of the Asian people and, indeed, I fear has driven them largely into the arms of Soviet Russia. Yet I am convinced that neither China nor any of these Asians will become or remain a mere puppet of Russia or any other European or American nation whether it be communist or capitalist. Undoubtedly
The Address-Mr. Coldwell the present government of China is a communist dictatorship which has won the present support of the depressed masses of China because it has instituted the land and other reforms which a western-supported democratic regime should have instituted and might have instituted if we had encouraged its formation against the corrupt regime of Chiang Kai-shek. Hon. members will recall that a few years ago General Marshall came back from China and suggested that we do that very thing. He said there were democratic leaders in China and he urged support for them instead of the arming of Chiang Kai-shek, as was done.
Since the banishment of Chiang all parties in the United Kingdom, realistically and in accordance with international precedents, have recognized the new regime in China. They do not approve of its ideology but they recognize a fact. I think we should have done the same thing, and even now I have come to the conclusion that if we are going to negotiate it would be wise for us to do so, because, if negotiations with China for peace in Korea are to be undertaken, the very fact of negotiations among civil governmental leaders implies, and indeed requires, recognition of their governmental status.
Once peace was achieved, then Canada could support the admission of the Peking government to the United Nations, as I imagine other countries would, and urge a general settlement of Asian problems, including self-determination by the native population of Formosa, in the interests of the Asian people and the peace of the world. As a matter of fact, if you are going to negotiate a peace with the present Chinese government, if you recognize that government as you would do in fact, then under the charter of the United Nations someone when peace has been attained has to represent China in the United Nations assembly; and having recognized the new regime in China, as you would have to do if you made peace with it, it is that regime that would have to be given a seat in the United Nations.

speechtext:
I do not think the hon. gentleman was following me. I am sure he knows that negotiations are in progress today between the United Nations and China. We are a partner in that war. I am suggesting that since there is a military stalemate in Korea, those nations which are actually suffering, losing their men and expending their treasure, should endeavour to negotiate an end to that stalemate. Then if peace were attained part of the vast expenditures we are making for war in the Far East could and should be used to provide economic and technical aid for the peoples of Asia. I want to say, as I have said so often before, that only in this way are we eventually going to defeat communism and communist propaganda.
Meantime we should not permit ourselves to be dominated by such policies as Mr. Dulles advocates for the United States. While it is difficult to say, as a matter of fact, what the policies in the United States really are on the whole, a statement such as the one I have quoted clearly indicates that if certain people obtain control in that country there is a danger of provoking a war with China and thus opening wide the door to communist domination of the world. As I have already said, however, the immediate problem is to end hostilities in Korea, and certainly no minor considerations should be allowed to prevent that. If the suggestion I have made for high level political negotiations were accepted another result would (low; that is, the position of Russia would be clarified. If Russia demanded the right to participate in armistice negotiations by the political leaders of the nations I have suggested should take a hand in it, Russia certainly could not claim the right to participate subsequently as a neutral nation in supervising the armistice, and that would clarify the position.
I have spent more time tonight in dealing with these matters than I intended because one of them was raised this afternoon by the leader of the opposition, and I wanted to place my views before the house as clearly as I could and, I may add, after having given

the matter a good deal of consideration. No one knows better than I that if communism should win a victory in the world, among its first victims would be the people who generally hold the views I hold on economic and social policies. Democratic socialists have been the first casualties when communist governments have been established in European countries, so I am under no illusions as far as that goes.
Now I want to turn to a domestic matter. I can cover only two or three points this evening because my time is limited and I usually like to cover a subject fairly thoroughly. To turn to this domestic matter, which I think is of great importance, we recollect that last June the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) informed this house that the government would give consideration to the establishment of a committee at this session to inquire once again into the question of health insurance. A few days ago he said the government had considered the matter and that such a committee would not be established.
Last summer we saw no real necessity for such a committee. Surely by this time and after all these years the government has all the information necessary and should be prepared to introduce legislation for the establishment, in co-operation with the provinces, of a plan that would be comprehensive and, I would suggest, which would be on the basis of the completion of a general social security plan. Yet apparently in the opinion of the government another inquiry seems to-be a necessary prelude to any definite action. Even last June the promise of another committee reminded us that the Liberal party had promised us health insurance in its platform of 1919. That was 33 years ago.

maintopic: CO-OPERATIVE ORGANIZATIONS REQUEST FOR INCORPORATION OF NATIONAL SOCIETY    PROCEDURE IN QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman says we should give them time. Perhaps for the Liberal party a third of a century is not sufficient time to carry out some of its promises. Again, before the election of 1945 a parliamentary committee had actually recommended legislation which people in various parts of Canada were told would be enacted if the government were returned to power. This was particularly true in my own province where the present provincial leader, Mr. Tucker, who had been chairman of the committee, exhibited a draft bill which had been, printed and circulated among members of this house-it was not his bill; it was circulated here-and the statement was made that it was certain of enactment if the government were returned. Nothing has been, heard of that bill since.

In 1948, prior to three important federal by-elections the former prime minister, Mr. King, in announcing the health grants program, which we welcomed, described it as the first step in a national health plan. Because of all this I am going to move an amendment dealing with this matter, in these words:
That the following words be added to the amendment:
"This house further regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to recommend the inauguration of a national health insurance program, with provision for provincial participation."
Over the years a good many investigations have been made and a good many commissions established. Every commission appointed to investigate health in Canada has without exception testified to the need for health insurance. For example, the royal commission on health insurance and maternity benefits in British Columbia in 1932; governmental commissions on health and medical services in Alberta in 1933 and 1944; a report of the Quebec social insurance commission; the special committee on social security set up by the federal parliament in 1943, to which I have already referred; the federal government's own proposals to the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction after the war-all these have agreed on the necessity for national health insurance. They all found that the average citizen is unable to provide adequate medical care for himself and his family if he is left to depend upon his own resources.
In addition, various groups throughout the country representing workers, farmers, business and professional men and so on, have made representations to the government asking for health insurance. Nine years ago, in 1943, the parliamentary committee to which I have already referred heard 117 witnesses representing 32 different groups. Each group expressed itself in favour of the principle of health insurance. Despite all these expert testimonials from groups representing every segment of our society; in spite of this research by competent personnel over the years; in spite of the government's own reports and investigations, the government still dallies while the social and economic costs for want of health insurance mount daily.
What are the reasons for this delay? One of the favourite excuses is that the federal government has not yet been able to reach a satisfactory agreement with all the provinces. Difficulties involved in making financial and administrative arrangements have been given as the reason for failure to achieve such an agreement. But these difficulties have been given before as excuses
The Address-Mr. Coldwell for delaying in various fields; yet when public pressure for action has become strong enough the government has generally succeeded in finding a way around these difficulties. If I may, I should like to quote the late Dr. Harry Cassidy, director of the Toronto School of Social Work, who said:
The conclusion emerges that the dominion-provincial relations controversy is far less of a barrier to national social security policy than is commonly supposed ... A dominion government which was firmly committed to prompt action on social security could almost certainly do much to achieve results.
Constitutional difficulties should not be allowed to stand in the way of health legislation for all Canadians. There is no reason why the federal government cannot provide health insurance legislation to become effective in each province as that province adopts enabling legislation. In this way health insurance would become effective across the country as quickly as the various provinces passed the necessary legislation. This is the procedure now being followed with respect to the Old Age Assistance Act. Some provinces have yet to reach agreement with the federal government; but no one would contend for a moment that those provinces which have made agreements with the federal government should have to wait until all provinces reach accord.
The same thing is true with regard to health insurance. The whole country should not be held up, waiting for adequate health legislation, until unanimous agreement is secured with all the provinces. Indeed the government itself in 1945 proposed to the dominion-provincial conference that the health insurance plan be capable of introduction as each province was ready. The federal government should get on with the job of instituting a plan in which all the provinces could co-operate.
Since my time is just about exhausted, I want to skip along and to say this in conclusion. The costs of poor health to society, as well as to the individual, are staggering. When, for example, sickness strikes the breadwinner of a family, it impairs the income of that family, and consequently in many instances the burden must be assumed by society as a whole. But how often could such sickness have been prevented in the first place if adequate preventive medical care had been assured without the worry of financial difficulties. Again, in the case of industry, countless production time is lost every year simply because preventive medicines and medical care could not be afforded by the wage earners.
The question, then, is not whether we can afford to have health insurance but whether

The Address-Mr. Low we can afford not to have it. It is my belief, and that of those associated with me in the C.C.F., that we cannot afford to continue with our haphazard and inadequate method of meeting the health needs of Canadians.
At the last session of parliament we urged that provision be made for a national health plan which would include hospitalization, medical care and health insurance. I regret to say, however, that not only the government but also the other two opposition parties combined to defeat our motion on the ground-and I will state it-that our amendment made no mention of provincial participation. We intended that it should be so oonstrued. That provision was certainly not in that amendment, but it is in this one. The C.C.F. believes that a national health insurance program is the only way by which the nation's health can be adequately protected. Furthermore, we believe that the vast majority of the Canadian people are in favour of such legislation. We have therefore moved this amendment in order to bring this matter before the house and ensure a discussion of the subject. I hope that ere long we shall have in Canada a complete social security system including all that national health services involve.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words must be of congratulation to the mover (Mr. George) and the seconder (Mr. Gauthier, Lake St. John) of the address in reply. In my judgment both of those gentlemen acquitted themselves well. From their speeches I gathered a great deal of most useful information, more particularly about their own home constituencies. I may say, sir, that that is a matter about which I did not know a great deal. With the subject matter of the speeches one would not expect me to agree entirely, and I shall have something to say about a few of the things that have been mentioned by the mover, at least.
We have already expressed our feeling of great regret and sorrow at the loss of our late beloved sovereign. At this time I can only say that our group in the house are in thorough agreement with the first two paragraphs in His Excellency's address. We have expressed our allegiance and our devotion to our new sovereign. I shall therefore not take the time now to go further into the matter.
The speech of His Excellency contained some exceedingly interesting items, amongst a miscellaneous grab-bag assortment of petits, if we want to call them that. I should like, however, to pass over the smaller things and take up for a few minutes some of those that I look upon as being very important.
(Mr. Coldwell.]
One of the first of those is this. In the past few days much has been said about the unfortunate outbreak in the province of Saskatchewan of that terrible foot-and-mouth disease. For that reason I do not intend to say much at this time except to point out that the farmers of the west are now suffering a second great blow-as, in fact, are the farmers of all Canada, for that matter-as a result of the outbreak of this terrible disease. But the farmers of the west especially are now suffering a double blow in that they still have 150 million bushels of wheat unharvested and perhaps 135 million bushels of oats and barley. Many of these farmers are going to find the coming season exceedingly difficult to finance. Our sympathies certainly go out to those farmers who are going to lose a great deal of money obtained by their hard-earned efforts over the years to accumulate something with which to make themselves secure.
I want to say that we appreciate the steps which the government has taken to compensate the farmers who are going to lose directly through having their herds of cattle destroyed. I want to join the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in an expression of optimism in this regard. I have every hope and every reason to believe that, through prompt and efficient action, the government will get this disease under control and stamp it out. I think nothing short of a complete stamping out of the disease is good enough in a country that has gone on for so many decades free from this terrible scourge.
One thing I should like to stress in concluding my remarks on this particular subject is that I hope the government will explore every possibility of extending in the British isles the market for our beef, pork and surplus meat. If they do that, they are going to have to be prepared to take British goods in payment, and they will have to take quite a different view with respect to embargoes or high dumping duties on automobiles from Britain. A far different attitude will have to be adopted if we expect to find and to hold anything like a market in Great Britain. We should see to it that the people there get these products of ours, and that our farmers and the general public in this country are not called upon to suffer because we have neglected the potential markets that can be found in that country.
We were greatly gratified to see in His Excellency's speech that provision would be made for an amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act of 1946 and the Veterans Benefit Act of 1951. I think that hon. members should hang their heads in shame for having

allowed so many of those old veterans to go through the past winter-yes, 1 could say several winters-living on the miserable pittance which they had been allowed under the act when the Canadian dollar was really worth something. The sacrifices that those old veterans made for all of us were great. I have often wondered why, in the light of these sacrifices, they should have been left so long struggling and trying to make ends meet on this miserable pittance, particularly since hon. members on every side of the house have pressed for action to enlarge those allowances. The money certainly was available in our country, and production sufficient to guarantee those old veterans certain standards of comfort beyond what we have been giving them. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my group I welcome the assurance that something is to be done at this session. We also express the hope that it will be something substantial, to bring these veterans at least up to something like the parity of other veterans with respect to allowances.
I now turn to another subject, Mr. Speaker. The mover of the address said that this is the first time that anyone had moved an address to one of Canada's native sons. That is true. The same hon. gentleman did not say, though, whether he agreed with this departure from traditional practice. I gathered that he accepted it without protest. I wish it definitely understood, Mr. Speaker, that in what I shall say here today I have no quarrel whatever with the present appointee who represents the queen in Canada. Undoubtedly the Right Hon. Vincent Massey is perfectly capable of doing an excellent job in this, high office. In my judgment he is an illustrious gentleman, and I have nothing whatever to say against him. Rather, sir, it is with the principle of the whole question that I quarrel. My own feeling is that the government, without consulting parliament, in addition to what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) said about arrogating to themselves the right to change the constitution in various forms, designations and titles that have become traditional practice over the decades, has also taken the first step to bring the highest symbolic office in the land down to the realm of contentious politics, and consequently the constitutional system that we have been operating under for so many years might be seriously damaged. I believe it would have been far better to have kept the holders of this high and important office completely free from political influences, at least as long as there are already so many other things which might adversely affect the spirit of unity in Canada.
The Address-Mr. Low
Some distinguished person from any other part of the commonwealth would have been completely free from political influences in Canada and therefore, in my judgment, would have been a unifying force in Canadian life, as well as a factor in strengthening the ties of commonwealth. By its action, however, this government has injected one more possible cause for division amongst our people, one more cause for contention, and perhaps-I hope not-bitter political strife.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has attempted to justify his action in appointing a Canadian to the office of governor general by citing Australia as an example. Well, I do not need to remind the Prime Minister or anybody else that Australia is not Canada. The same conditions do not prevail in the two countries, and that has to be kept in mind.
It seems that the Prime Minister considered a departure from the traditional way of appointing a governor general to be a logical step in the normal development of Canada from the status of a colony to that of a self-governing dominion. Well, I should like to draw his attention, as did the leader of the opposition this afternoon, by way of underlining what was said, to the fact that there is in Canada a very large body of people who look upon this last move as the last straw in a series of moves which this government has taken with almost indecent haste to destroy every evidence of our British connection and our allegiance to the crown. Whether they are correct or not, Mr. Speaker, the fact remains that there are many who have that feeling and I have received petition after petition, communication after communication, drawing this to my attention and asking that something be done to put a stop to this series of steps lest we sever completely our allegiance to the crown. That is the way they expressed it to me. The Prime Minister will find, when he goes to the country in a general election, that his Liberal party certainly has not won votes through the series of steps that have been taken.
In the person of Lord Alexander Canada had a brilliant and beloved governor general. He did perhaps more than any other holder of the office up to this time to oring unity amongst the Canadian people. He set, in my judgment, a very high standard of performance which it will be quite difficult for anyone who follows him to measure up to. Our warmest wishes go with Lord Alexander and his family, all of whom have endeared themselves to the Canadian people. At the same time, sir, I should like to assure His

The Address-Mr. Low Excellency, our new governor general, of our good will, and I would like to take this opportunity of wishing him success, happiness, and complete satisfaction throughout the whole of his term of office.

I should now like to turn for just a few minutes to the consideration of another matter which has been occupying the minds of a good many Canadians of late. I think the leader of the opposition acquitted himself very well this afternoon in speaking about this whole matter. I may repeat one or two things that he said. I believe it would be well to underline the importance of this whole matter of piling up surpluses out of taxation at a time like this. I am not going to cover the whole of the ground, but I want to say something that the leader of the opposition did not say. I would like to ask for just one minute, what is the meaning of this over $700 million surplus, about which we have heard so much? Well, if it is reduced to its simplest terms it means that the people of Canada have had to dig down and surrender to this government in the form of direct and indirect taxes over $700 million more in nine months of this fiscal year than the government figured it needed for the whole year. When this huge total is reduced to an individual basis, as the leader of the opposition said this afternoon, it means that the government confiscated-and that is the only word that I can find for it-confiscated from every man, woman and child in Canada $52 more than actually needed to be taken from them for balancing the government's budget this year. That means, as the leader of the opposition also pointed out, that every family of four therefore would be victimized to the extent of $208 extra taxation.
When I criticize the government for this extra taxation, let me make it clear, sir, that I do not think it is good business at a time like this to budget for deficits. I am with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in that. I do not think it would be wise at all, and I do not advocate budgeting for deficits. I go further than that and say I think under present circumstances it is a good thing for the minister to budget for a surplus; but when I say that I mean a modest surplus. I am not unmindful, however, of the great difficulties which are faced by the Minister of Finance. Actually it is certainly difficult in the midst of present conditions to forecast with anything like accuracy either what revenues might be obtained or what the rate of expenditure might be, particularly in the field of defence preparations. I am quite
[Mr. Low.l
mindful of that. The Minister of Finance has some excuse, therefore, in not being able to estimate more closely than he has done.
Moreover, the minister, in my judgment, was on sound ground when he said, as he did in his radio broadcast on February 19,
I believe it was, that it was fortunate that he was able to have some surplus cash to take care of such things as defence and the Canadian National Railways, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the foreign exchange control board so as to obviate the necessity of borrowing more money from the chartered banks. Well, borrowing from the chartered banks would have been inflationary. I think anyone who knows anything about finance knows that. But I suppose it is nice even for the average Canadian individual to have some surplus cash around, just as it is for the government. As a matter of fact, the Minister of Finance said that he thought it was nice to have surplus cash around so that he could stockpile such things as wool, rubber, tin and other materials for use in the defence program.
I agree with him. But at the same time let me say that it is also nice for the average individual Canadian to have surplus cash around so that he can stockpile some things, too. But the Minister of Finance has seen to it that the individual Canadian has not got it, because the minister has taken it away. And there are literally hundreds of thousands of them who have not got enough to live decently on these days.

Everybody is glad to see the government making an effort to get out of debt. I think it is especially gratifying to the Canadian citizen to see his government attempting to get out of debt, especially if he thinks they have sense enough to stay out when they do get out. But there are times when the government is not justified in confiscating the people's purchasing power merely to pay off debts. This is one of those times.
The government is indifferent, completely indifferent, to the welfare of the Canadian

people, when it piles up a huge surplus and revenue through the use of taxation, and especially through the use of taxation of the kind used by the Minister of Finance, when indirect or hidden taxes are inevitably pushing up prices and the cost of living.
So when the minister says, "I used $310 million"-that is the amount, I believe- "to pay off debt", as one justification for having the surplus, then I say to the house that he was completely unjustified in taking that taxation from the people this year to pay off that debt.
I join with the leader of the opposition in his protest against it. There are times, appropriate and suitable times, when that sort of thing should be done. But I do not subscribe to the idea of allowing the Minister of Finance to set up a huge surplus and then, when he is embarrassed about it, find a place quickly to get it out of the way, and then come before the Canadian people and say he is using it to pay off the debt.
It seems to me the real criticism of the Minister of Finance is that he piled up his surplus largely through his hidden taxes- that is, excise taxes, sales taxes and others. These very definitely pyramid prices and in many cases they go away beyond, or inflate prices away beyond the amount of revenue that the government receives from the imposition of the taxes.
The Minister of Finance argued that by using some of the surplus to pay off the debt he has saved the Canadian people considerably more money in interest. Well, that is so. I agree. But what earthly use is it to save the people interest if, by the very means taken by the minister to save interest, he causes the people to pay more in the form of higher prices than the amount of interest saved? That is a question I would like the minister to answer-or indeed anyone else to answer.
Of the $310 million of debt paid off from the surplus so far this year accumulated, the people have been saved perhaps $9,300,000 in interest.
But the taxes responsible for the raising of the $310 million surplus revenue have increased prices and the cost of living to the people of Canada to the extent of at least 30 per cent of the $310 million or, in round figures, $90 million. I do not think anyone can deny that that is so.

On February 29 the Canadian Chamber of Commerce submitted to the Minister of Finance a brief regarding the government's taxation and fiscal policy. On page 5 of the submission this is stated:
We strongly and frankly believe that even the present levels are too high and should be reduced to a point where personal and corporate efficiency can again be stimulated.

The third point I should like to make about taxes is in regard to the hidden indirect taxes which the government have imposed and which they cling to so tenaciously. They have caused and are causing very serious loss in the spending power of many of the people of Canada. Take as one example an electric iron, and there are many more examples that could be cited. Let us take one that is made in the United States, as a good many of these electric irons are. Let us assume that the factory cost is $5, which is just about the usual level. What happens to that factory price of $5 by the time the iron reaches the consumer here in Canada?
There is a duty of 224 per cent on the iron, which increases the price by $1.12, making it $6.12. I pass on to my concluding subject. His Excellency's address reminds us, and I quote:
The situation throughout the world continues to cause concern and to require my ministers to devote a great deal of attention to our external affairs. The government remains convinced that the nations of the free world must continue to increase their combined strength, in order to ensure lasting peace and security by the effective discouragement of aggression.
Commenting on this topic, the mover of the address (Mr. George) used these words, and I quote from page 24 of Hansard of February 29:
The Right Hon. Winston Churchill reminded us, in his Ottawa speech, that our own Prime Minister had a major share in building the North Atlantic treaty.
I acknowledge that that is true. But of late I have often wondered if when he first put forward his proposal for the formation of a North Atlantic alliance he envisioned some of the things that were bound to happen. I wonder, for example, if he envisioned and hoped that NATO would put the United Nations into an eclipse. Only a very dim-witted person could fail to see how immeasurably more important than the United Nations the North Atlantic Treaty Organization has become. I often wonder if the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), when he proposed the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, did not stop to realize that powerful forces would conspire to use the organization as a ramp to catapult us and other free nations into

The Address-Mr. Low federal union and world government which under present circumstances could only succeed in plunging us into an all-out world conflict, and perhaps even worse. The forces that itch and yearn for an early realization of the dream of world government feel quite sure that out of a new global conflict would emerge a world dictatorship modelled after that of the Soviet union.
Well, there are powerful forces which are conspiring and feverishly working to use the North Atlantic Treaty Organization for just that very purpose. Because they see their propaganda bearing fruit and their plans successfully advanced step by step, their exultation frequently causes them to become bold and in that boldness sometimes they overplay their hands. Many of their innocent supporters and willing collaborators are naive enough to let the cat out of the bag so that once in a while we can get a glimpse of just what is going on behind the scenes.
Only recently a fellow by the name of Ted Leather-I sometimes think his name should have been "Hell For Leather"-a member of parliament in Great Britain-

speechtext:
-exultantly declared over the B.B.C. and in various correspondence columns that Britain is now too feeble to safeguard the commonwealth and that she must therefore prepare to relinquish to a supranational authority control over her own foreign policy and defence. Mr. Leather is a Canadian. He explains his support of the proposal to use NATO as a ramp to catapult the free nations into a federal union by saying that he wishes to "conserve humanity" and "to ensure them peace". Both of these are childish pretensions on Mr. Leather's part. If the plan is to succeed, of course it is necessary to get over to Britons, Canadians and others the conviction that federal union or world government is the only way to save humanity and to bring them peace. It is also necessary to disseminate amongst the people of the present sovereign democracies the same kind of lie Mr. Leather attempts to spread far and wide over the B.B.C. in Britain, namely, that the British people are no longer capable of conducting their own foreign policy and defence.
I imagine Mr. Leather repeats this falsehood in pure innocence. But it seems to me there are two mysteries about it. The first of these mysteries is why he, a Canadian, should have sought and secured election to the parliament of Britain as, in the words of one correspondent, "the hot gospeller of a doctrine, rank with the smell of subversion". The second mystery is how a member of parliament manages to reconcile his oath of allegiance to his sovereign not only with silly

sneers at national sovereignty but also with his espousal of a cause that would subordinate and subjugate both our sovereign, Queen Elizabeth II, and her peoples to a cosmopolitan combination of power addicts. That is what it would mean. I often wonder why such people as Mr. Leather do not make an outright transfer of their allegiance to the new Atlantis and become in very fact the citizens of the world which they yearn to become. Perhaps they would soon find, as did young Garry Davis, that they were citizens of nowhere, or perhaps, like the original international communists I remember as a boy who tried to make themselves citizens of the world proletariat, they would have to find themselves a substitute motherland. Everybody who knows anything about history knows that the international communists found their motherland in the Soviet union. Even Tim Buck, sheltered, nourished and given freedom and opportunity by Canada, acknowledges the Soviet union as his motherland. He is apparently one of the contradictions of the old saying, "Even a louse clings to the flesh on which it feeds."
To come back to Mr. Leather, in his frothings over the B.B.C. he cited as his hero and exemplar what he called "Canada's great foreign secretary, Lester Pearson, who is the greatest advocate of such internationalism developing along the lines of NATO". So Clarence Streit is not the only one who claims our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) is a prominent leader in this move to establish world government through NATO. Leather and his pals look upon our Secretary of State for External Affairs as the giant, the demi-god from the west who comes to give peace to the historic nations of Europe. The ludicrousness of that situation may not have occurred to some people. Just imagine if you can a more ludicrous way of giving peace to the historic nations of Europe than by the simple device of extinguishing them completely. Stop and think about it.
On February 26, 1951, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart), in what I said was a very eloquent speech, moved a resolution in the following terms:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of supporting the calling of a convention of delegates from the democracies which sponsored the North Atlantic treaty and representing the principal political parties of such democracies, for the purpose of exploring how far their peoples, and the peoples of such other democracies as the convention may invite to send delegates, can apply among them, within the framework of the United Nations, the principles of federal union.
He left no doubt about what it was he then advocated, namely, the use of NATO to slide the free democracies into first, Atlantic federal union, and next, full world

government with an end to what he called "the myth of national sovereignty." Immediately following the hon. member for Winnipeg North, the Secretary of State for External Affairs spoke, and the more I reread his speech and consider it the more firm I become in my belief that it was a warning to the hon. member for Winnipeg North to lay off the subject for the time being because more careful groundwork would have to be done before the people would be ready and sufficiently anaesthetized to part with their sovereignty. At any rate, that ended the debate, for the hon. member for Winnipeg North withdrew his resolution.
Since February 26, 1951, a number of important things have transpired in this same field of activity. First, the NATO council met in Ottawa last summer, and prominent amongst the council's deliberations was consideration of ways and means of achieving the fullest possible integration of the western nations. The meetings were held in private. In fact every effort was made to keep them secret. However, through the shrouds of secrecy information conveniently-and I use that word advisedly-seeped through to the world press. Moreover, recommendations were broadcast long before the various governments who make up NATO had been made aware of them in any form. Someone disclosed some pretty secret information to Clarence Streit who rushed into print in his Freedom and Union magazine the news that the NATO council was to urge that the Atlantic community should be unified-and I use his words-"not only militarily as heretofore but politically, economically, socially and culturally, and that Mr. Acheson, United States foreign secretary, had given the proposals warm words of approval".
It should be remembered that Mr. Streit was one of the advocates of one world and world government who used the German scare, as they are now using the Russian scare, to try to stampede the Atlantic countries into a political union. Mr. Streit in his article in the October, 1951, issue of the Freedom and Union magazine was able to furnish the very confidential information that the Atlantic council had appointed a committee to carry the matter further. The committee, he said, consisted of Messrs, van Zeeland, de Gasperi, Stikker, Lange and Lester Pearson.
I spoke somewhat about all this in the house on October 22 last. There followed, I am told, some consternation amongst the faithful and devoted. Plans were laid for a visit to Ottawa of some prominent federal unionists from congress and various parts of the United States, a visit, I am told, which was scheduled for this spring. It will be
The Address-Mr. Low interesting to learn what procedure they advocate now to keep the people so intent on watching in fear the dark international picture that they will not notice the evolution of Atlantic federal union out of the present balance of power alliance called NATO.
I should like to conclude on this note. When I spoke on this matter on October 22 last I called upon the Secretary of State for External Affairs to declare in the most unequivocal terms exactly what are the long-range objectives of NATO, but to this date I have not heard that declaration. The Canadian people want to know where this government is leading our country. They are entitled to a full and detailed answer without delay. For us in this party, we favour the greatest possible measure of co-operation amongst the democracies for all worthy and righteous purposes. These purposes would include collective defensive measures as a means of preventing aggressive warfare that might lead to world conflict, or that might endanger the security of any or all of those nations. We support fully every effective effort to build the strongest possible integrated military force in western Europe for the prevention of aggression. But we are unalterably opposed to any nefarious or open attempt to bring about the political and economic integration of the NATO countries under a supranational government. We value too highly the liberties for which our fathers before us fought and bled and died. Above all we value and will do all in our power to preserve inviolate the right and liberty of every man to worship Almighty God in his own church in his own way, and the liberty to take an unimpaired part in his own government. We call upon all Canadians to make themselves thoroughly aware of what is going on around them, and prepare themselves to resist any effort to diminish or take away these and others of their precious freedoms.

Not long ago I was asked why the Canadian dollar is now on a par with the United States dollar or perhaps a little better, and I tried to set out the reasons. In the first place I would say the government of Canada was the chief reason. The opposition may not say so, but they think it just the same. A government that has been sane, secure and serviceable has done a great job. It has been telling the world that people who live in Canada will be properly taken care of.
Then there is our surplus. The United States has no surplus. Great Britain has no surplus. France has no surplus, except of ex-premiers. We in Canada have a surplus, and I will give the particulars a little later on. There is our expanding trade. I do not need to speak on that further; the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) can tell you all about it. That is one of the main reasons the government of Ontario is supporting the St. Lawrence waterway.
The next reason is the absence of labour troubles in Canada today. There is co-operation perhaps better than ever between management and labour. At Fort William we have outstanding examples of this co-operation in several firms that employ a good many people. Because of our growing industry we have been attracting people from the country
[Mr Mclvor.]
to the south and from other parts of the world who have money they want to invest in Canada.
Another reason our dollar has risen in value is the announcement by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) that we are going it alone in building the St. Lawrence waterway. The Minister of Trade and Commerce told a group in Washington a short time ago, "We are not bluffing this time." Other reasons the dollar has risen are Alberta and Saskatchewan oil, British Columbia and Ontario mining such as Steep Rock, and the development going on in Labrador. Any country with all these activities is bound to raise its head high above the other nations of the world.
People in other lands are beginning to recognize the government of Canada. On the front page of a local newspaper this evening you will see that two of the members of our government are mentioned for the Nobel peace prize. This shows that they have been outstanding; and they are not the only men in the cabinet who have attracted world attention.
I know that taxation is high, and I have not met anyone-I am not one-who likes to pay taxes. I would rather give a man a dollar to buy a meal or something else he wanted than pay taxes. But I expect that some taxes will come down. However, we must pay our way, and when the country is prosperous we must pay off our war debts. Through the kindness of the office of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) I obtained some figures, though I am not an expert on figures and usually get them mixed up. But during the year ending March 31, 1947, the government paid $373,600,000. In 1948 it paid $676,100,000; in 1949, $595,500,000.
