I saw another thing in Vancouver, namely the greatest bottleneck in traffic that I ever saw; it was at the south side of the Marpole bridge that leads to Sea island where there is the busiest airfield in Canada. I will say that subject to correction. That is the report that I received from Vancouver. One afternoon when we were trying to find our way through, there was a bottleneck of cars over a mile long. My friend, who was a major in the Salvation Army, told me that I was modest, that it was far more than a mile. Those cars had to move just a little bit at a time. I hope that the members from Vancouver, Liberal, Conservative or something else, the city council of Vancouver and the provincial members will see to it that those working people on Sea island are treated just as well as are the rich in any other part of Vancouver. So much for the bottleneck.
I have some things to say about Fort William. I do not think there is a better place than the lakehead for a young couple to build a home and have a family, and train them in the Christian way. I do not know of a better place for that purpose than Fort William and Port Arthur. The reason for this is that the churches there are alive and are looking after not only the old people and those who have money; and the ministers are not conspicuous as men who keep their eyes on the collection plate. They are men who keep their eyes on the youth when they are growing up, and they are doing a great job.
I have spoken before about the way in which our youth in Fort William are taken care of. Because the city of Ottawa has a mayor who has an interest in recreation for
The Address-Mr. Mclvor the youth, and because difficulty has been experienced in handling their recreation in Ottawa, I thought that the mayor of Ottawa and the city council could well send a delegation .to the lakehead and see how things are done there. They could then come back and people would have ears for them.
During the summer we have supervised playgrounds. This is the result of the work of those of us who thought there should be playgrounds; but the thing was done voluntarily and sometimes the workers were absent. We have a superintendent of parks, and I do not mind using his name. He is Mr. Art Widnall. He is a Conservative but he is decent just the same. He takes a group of high school pupils and trains them for about a month in how to lead young people, boys and girls, in recreation and at the same time gets some sense into their heads. This is done during the months of July and August. Then during the winter we have supervised hockey rinks. We have 24 supervised hockey rinks. There is a rink for hockey and alongside there is another one for skating. Those are the best places you can look at. If you keep boys busy with their hands and feet, the police will not need to take care of them. In fact, one of our big policeman is one of the outstanding leaders of our boys at these hockey rinks.
We have two large swimming pools. Then we have the Kam river where some of us like to go quite often because of the fine swimming and the clean water which is available. We have twenty pee-wee teams, six bantam, five midget, four juvenile and two junior teams in Fort William and two in Port Arthur, and one senior team. Our senior team this year is the champion one of the district. The Minister of Trade and Commerce
(Mr. Howe) would agree with me, I think_____
although I have not consulted him on it-that the lakehead is perhaps one of the best places in Canada today for the setting up of new industries. We have power, shipping and railroads. In Fort William we have the best water system in Canada. The water is obtained from a big lake, 800 feet up on mount McKay, and all they had to do was to put down a viaduct or hole through the rock and the power of the water coming down was sufficient for their purpose. They did not need any engine here. The water is pure, clean and fresh. In our community we have two men whom I should like to mention. We have the provincial man who takes care of the farmers. We have the dominion man who takes care of the agriculture substations. Those two men do an outstanding job in inspiring our youth in the belief that there is no occupation, except the ministry, that is preferable to the life on the farm; and they

The Address-Mr. Mclvor are doing it in such a way that the young men are taking hold of the farms. I pay my tribute to these two men. They have potato clubs, oat clubs and seed clubs. The meetings of those seed clubs are well attended and they are doing a great job.
We have some needs. The Fort William sanatorium received a grant from the former minister of national health and welfare, now Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). The grant has been continued by the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). It amounted to $200,000 for the sanatorium. We had then 75 Indians in that sanatorium. We have more than doubled it now, and the sanatorium needs more money. They come to the local member and say that they need more money, and I agree with them, and we are going to try to get it.
Another need in Fort William has to do with mount McKay. Mount McKay is an outstanding asset to our city, and would be more so if it were used as a national park. We have a great ski jump there. There is natural skiing quite a distance back and all around. I am told that by the boys and girls. I do not use skis, and I do not skate very often. They tell me that there are great slides on mount McKay, as great as there are anywhere else in Canada, but the Indians own mount McKay. I am telling the minister that a delegation will be here shortly, and we shall call on him a little later on.
We have another need for industry and that is a breakwater in front of island No. 2, but I am not going to enlarge on that now. We need that for the pulp and paper industry and our saw mills and as protection for our logs.
In closing I want to say a word on the world situation. We believe in democracy and we believe in freedom, the right kind of freedom. The new chancellor of Victoria university, the Hon. L. B. Pearson, in his address to the students, called attention to the battle of ideas now going on in the modern world. He said:
Communism could never be killed by bayonets. It must be met with intellectual and spiritual weapons and1 by removing the conditions of poverty and misery in which it grows.
He went on to say:
Freedom must include the obligation to be socially useful, and to struggle against evil and injustice. Only on that concept of freedom can a free and secure society be based.
We have not very many atheists in Canada; we have some, men who do not believe in God. I received a letter a little while ago.

I read a few sentences of it and I looked down to see who was writing it. He confessed himself in his opening remarks that he was an atheist, but he did not sign the letter and I did not finish reading it. I say to hon. members: If you get an anonymous letter never read it. It will not do you any good and it will not hurt the other fellow very much either. According to the history of the world any country that leaves out its faith in God soon falls. What happened in the first war? What happened to Hitler? According to a prophet from the city of Chicago Russia will have a revolution. He said that two years ago. He said that they will have a revolution in Russia and the common people will be properly dealt with.
I deem it a great honour, Mr. Speaker, to be permitted to speak in this debate. I am sure we shall hear quite a few speeches and not very much repetition. If any hon. members happen to come down Fort William way, do not be afraid to drop in and we will treat you as becomes a progressive city. You will find, in and around Fort William, scenery that is second1 to none, even in the Rockies.

Mr. Speaker, as the newest member of this house, in the week since my introduction to the House of Commons I have been a most interested but a silent observer of proceedings. Now that the time has come to take a more vocal part, may I start by extending congratulations to the hon. members who moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne. May I say also that I greatly enjoyed listening to the addresses today by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the leaders of the other opposition parties. I might add, however, that I found myself much more in agreement with the views expressed on this side of the house than with the views expressed on the other side.
May I say in all seriousness that, on behalf of Calgary West, I should like to extend a word of appreciation to all hon. members for the tributes they paid last December to the memory of the late Arthur LeRoy Smith and for the messages of sympathy that came from all parts of this house to Sarah Smith.
As a member of parliament Art Smith served his country and his constituency well. He was undoubtedly one of the most popular and respected members of this parliament. He was one of the foremost citizens of our western country. As a parliamentarian, as a lawyer, as a humanitarian, as a common

man with the virtues and some of the failings of a common man, as a wit and as a proponent of common sense, Art Smith has left a rich legacy to our country.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the debate dealing with the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in southern Saskatchewan. This of course is a serious and a potentially disastrous blow to Canada's economy, a blow that has fallen just as hard on Alberta as on any other section of the country, although, fortunately, there has been no outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in my home province. I trust that the government under the new legislation will deal fairly and effectively with all those who have been economically affected adversely by the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease. I trust also that this government will deal effectively to prevent the spread of the disease to other parts of our country.
Alberta of course is one of the largest livestock raising provinces of our country. My home city, Calgary, is one of the great cattle centres of the nation. We are feeling in Alberta at the present time major adverse effects by the closing of the borders of the provinces to the east and to the west of Alberta and the closing of the United States border to the movement of cattle from Alberta and other Canadian provinces. In fact we in Alberta at the present time are in the unhappy position that our livestock is unable to move east, west or south. The only way open is north. I trust that if no other means are available the government will take all possible steps at least to convert the Eskimos of the north from blubber to beef.
There is another problem, and that is one which has already directly affected far more people than the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease. Out in Calgary we have taken to calling this particular malady Abbottitis. I might say to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that this name given to the malady, Abbottitis, does not indicate on the part of those in Calgary who have applied the name that the minister is the virus which is carrying this malady across the country, but merely that his name is the name most closely associated with its spread.
The symptoms of Abbottitis, of course, are well known to us all. They include loss of weight, in pocketbook and bank account; they include fraying tempers and fraying cuffs; they include declining living standards; they include bigger government surpluses and more inflation. The causes of Abbottitis might briefly be stated as errors in budgeting and 55704-13
The Address-Mr. Nickle excessive taxation. There will be considerable discussion later in this session as to the cure for this malady, and at that time I trust I may have an opportunity to say more about it.
In my week in the house I have heard a great deal about a number of other constituencies in our country. Fortunately, as the representative from Calgary West I do not need to devote much time to a discussion of what Calgary West contains by way of material resources and population. My predecessor in this office well advertised Calgary West. In fact we have in that constituency about 100,000 good public relations agents, including every man, woman and child in the constituency.
The west portion of the constituency of Calgary West covers Canada's finest mountain park; I refer of course to Banff national park. That park lies immediately to the south of Jasper national park. May I say that the residents of Banff national park have only one thing they would want to trade with Jasper, and that is their respective shares of the national parks annual appropriation.
Calgary itself is, as is well known, the centre of southern Alberta's agricultural industry. It is the greatest cattle centre in Alberta. It is also the centre of many other industries. The greatest of the new industries, now rated as Alberta's No. 2 industry, is that of petroleum and natural gas. I shall devote most of my comments this evening to imparting some information concerning that oil and gas industry. Before doing so however let me say this, that I call Calgary the centre of western Canada's oil and gas industry. Perhaps I should add to that that in recent years the home constituency of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) has developed into what we can now rightly call Canada's subsidiary oil capital-

speechtext:
-the major capital being, of course, the constituency I represent. The story of the oil and gas industry about which you have heard something from other speakers today-and you no doubt have read a good deal about it in the papers in recent months-had its beginning in my home city. It started many years ago, back in 1912, when a number of pioneering Calgarians, who were willing to take a gamble, stepped out and did some exploratory drilling along the banks of Sheep creek in Turner valley. From those early pioneer efforts, mainly by farmers,

The Address-Mr. Nickle ranchers and small businessmen in the Calgary district, came in time the discovery of Turner valley as Canada's and the British empire's first major oil and gas field.
There also came an awakening of interest on the part of large oil companies both inside and outside Canada in the oil and gas possibilities of Alberta. As a result, through the years, up to and including 1946, a large number of companies, big and small, carried out exploration operations in Alberta and other western provinces that consumed a total of something like $50 million.
From that program came a few small oil patches, several fairly large natural gas fields, two or three major gas fields-all in Alberta -but nothing of a size that justified the high hopes that had been held out by the opening up of Turner valley as the first major field.
Five years ago, in February of 1947, the picture changed, when Imperial Oil discovered the Leduc Devonian field southwest of Edmonton. I am going to give only a few figures that, I think, will convey something of the importance of the economic revolution that has taken place in Alberta and has spread beyond Alberta to other parts of Canada in the five years since the Leduc discovery. At the beginning of 1947 Alberta was producing 19,000 barrels of oil a day. It was producing less than 10 per cent of Canada's petroleum needs. Today western Canada-and of this, 95 per cent is in Alberta -has an oil potential exceeding 250,000 barrels of oil per day. The actual yield of oil during the last year ranged, with varying seasonal market conditions, from a low of 100,000 barrels to a high last fall of 168,000 barrels daily.
Right now, with the great lakes closed to winter shipping, our oil fields in the west are producing about 120,000 barrels of oil a day. Two months from now, with the opening of the great lakes, and the start of spring work on the prairies, there will be recorded for the first time a one-thousand-per-cent increase in oil production over that which prevailed at the time of the Leduc discovery. This spring, beginning in May and continuing through until the lakes are closed again in the fall, western Canada will be producing crude oil at a rate between 190,000 and 200,000 barrels a day. By mid-1954-and this is based upon what we know concerning present fields and reserves, and rate of development, and also includes an allowance for new discoveries, of which undoubtedly there will be many-western Canada will likely have an oil potential of at least 400,000 barrels per day, an amount

equal to the total demand of all Canada for that year. The actual yield in 1954, I might say, will likely be 280,000 barrels per day, year round, daily average. That figure is based upon the steps already taken, or now being taken, to provide transportation facilities and new refining facilities to make greater use of the oil in Canada's west.
Oil reserves five years ago were counted as 100 million barrels. Today western Canada can safely count its proved oil reserve at approximately 1,700 million barrels. In other words, there is an increase of something over 1,700 per cent in five years. I doubt whether any other Canadian industry has recorded as high a percentage increase in that period.
As to the future we can say only this, that there are in western Canada 400,000 square miles of geologically favourable territory for the accumulation of oil and gas. And of that huge total less than five per cent has been explored adequately.
Of those provinces outside of Alberta, let me say that western Canada's potential oil and gas region stretches from the United States border to the Arctic ocean, from the Rocky mountains clear through to the Canadian shield. In other words, it covers practically all of Alberta, the southern half of Saskatchewan, the southwest corner of Manitoba, the northeast section of British Columbia, and stretches up through the Northwest Territories along the Mackenzie river basin to the Arctic.
The other provinces also have petroleum hopes. Geologically favourable for oil and gas are such regions as western Ontario, where Canada's first oil was produced some 90 years ago; there is the James bay area of Ontario; there is the Gaspe peninsula of Quebec; there is the Moncton area of New Brunswick where a small oil and gas field has been producing for many years; and there are the provinces of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. There are also geologically favourable areas for oil and gas in Newfoundland and along the Pacific coast of British Columbia. Rich as it is in oil and gas, Alberta is not the only part of our dominion which offers prospects of oil wealth for our nation.
Natural gas is a subject which has become of considerable interest across the country in recent years. In the last five years in Alberta there have been over 125 new natural gas discoveries. Today our natural gas reserves in Alberta are estimated at somewhere between 8,000 billion and 12,000 billion cubic feet. As to the future, no one yet can predict with any degree of certainty just how much the ultimate gas reserves of Alberta or its

neighbouring province to the east will be. But this much is certain, that the rate of gas discovery is increasing and that geologists can still say with certainty that less than 5 per cent of the area geologically favourable for gas accumulation has been explored.
Many authorities are thinking in terms of self-sufficiency in oil for Canada and a large surplus of oil and gas for Canada's neighbours. My guess is that within a decade western Canada will be turning out oil and natural gas with a value greater than the output of western Canada's agricultural industry. That is making a big statement as agriculture today is a billion dollar per year industry. Last year the oil industry in the west produced only $120 million worth of oil and gas.
What is being done to achieve this rather happy state of national self-sufficiency? A few figures will perhaps be of interest to those outside my province. Last year for the sixth year in a row the oil industry set new records. More than two hundred companies poured more than $200 million into land, exploration and development of oil and gas prospects in western Canada.
They completed 1,370 wells, including 430 dry holes. It must be remembered that the oil industry is still a mighty risky one. In addition to the dry holes, there were a number of discoveries which dwarfed anything in previous years. There were in fact 108 discoveries of oil or gas made in the west last year alone. There were 40 oil discoveries [DOT]and 68 natural gas discoveries. The province of Alberta led with 98 discoveries made up of 35 oil and 63 gas. Saskatchewan came out with 5 discoveries last year. Manitoba came out with its first 2 discoveries. British Columbia came out with 2 discoveries in the northeast section of the province.
Today new records are still being set. In the first two months of this year there have been 15 discoveries of oil and gas in western Canada. In fact word came through yesterday of another quite important discovery, the second in Calgary West constituency, of wet gas at a point thirty miles northeast of Calgary. Another discovery ninety miles northeast of Calgary was reported last week end.
I should like to say a word about the spending rate. This government has been spending money at a tremendous rate for years so perhaps these figures may not appear to be much in terms of government spending. Private enterprise in western Canada-the oil and gas industry-is spending $12 million a month on drilling and geological and geophysical exploration. It is spending more millions monthly on land acquisition, lease and reservation rentals. The number of drilling rigs in operation in the west today
55704-13J
The Address-Mr. Nickle is 237, and the number is increasing month by month. Five years ago there were only 19 drilling rigs running. Of all the rigs in the west today, 89 are drilling wildcat wells seeking new oil or gas finds.
I may say that in terms of drilling rigs active, Canada is today No. 2 among all the world's nations.
Geophysical operations-including seismograph, gravitymeter, and magnetometer-are also proceeding at a record rate, looking for the structures which geologists consider worth drilling. There are now 157 of these geophysical parties roaming the west compared with no more than a dozen five years ago. Alberta has 130 of these geophysical parties; Saskatchewan has 19; Manitoba has 3 and British Columbia has 5. Of the drilling rigs, Alberta has 203; Saskatchewan has 23; Manitoba has 5 and British Columbia has 6. I may say that Saskatchewan, Manitoba and British Columbia are still in the early stages of exploration and development as compared with my home province of Alberta.
In the five years since the Leduc discovery started the modern oil boom $1,000 million or more in capital investment has been made. Over $500 million of that has gone into land exploration and development. The balance has gone into pipe lines, tankers, refineries and other facilities across the nation to provide the oil and gas industry in the west with the products and materials it needs.
There are certain coming events which will help to shape the destiny of the oil industry. One of these is the oil pipe line to the Pacific coast. Construction on that pipe line will start this spring and will be completed by the spring of 1954. The next coming event I believe will be an oil exchange program of some kind, to be worked out I trust by this government and the United States. It is only by means of an oil exchange program or something similar that Canada can reach self-sufficiency in petroleum. Far eastern markets are too far distant cost-wise from the oil fields of western Canada to be reached direct.
The next event may be approval by the Alberta government, which I trust will be soon, of export of natural gas. When gas export is approved this parliament will take on the responsibility of determining whether the east, the west or the south will get Alberta gas first. Another coming event is the growth of a large petrochemical industry in Alberta. No comments on oil and gas would be complete without a few words as to the benefits, direct and indirect, which stem from oil to the communities where oil has been found, and

The Address-Mr. NicJcle to the country as a whole. In Alberta the government owns 90 per cent of the mineral rights underlying the province. The government of that province has developed a formula which involves a minimum of risk and a maximum of profit for the treasury of the province. That formula has also given a fair share to those willing to explore or put up moneys for exploration. As a result, since the discovery of Leduc five years ago the Alberta treasury has reaped over $130 million in cash returns from oil and gas. I might say that from the oil and gas reserves on government lands in Alberta that are proved at the present time, royalties payable to the government and proceeds still to be received in bonuses from crown reserves sales and from rentals and fees will likely bring the Alberta treasury over the next decade at least another $500 million. This is not an invitation of course to the federal government to find some means of slapping a tax on the province of Alberta.
because of the lower cost petroleum products made available by Alberta oil. The fuel bill of the prairie provinces is now at least $50 million a year less than it would have been if it had not been for the displacement of higher cost foreign oil by the crude oils of Alberta.
At least as important as all the other benefits in these times of world struggle between communism and democracy is the building up of rich oil and gas reserves, transport and refining facilities and associated industries in the heart of the North American continent. These resources of western Canada are now a mighty weapon and will become an even more mighty one in the hands of Canada and her friends in waging and winning war against the evil forces lurking behind the iron curtain.

With respect to the other parts of the west, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and British Columbia have begun to collect exploration fees, rentals and royalties. They, like Alberta, are sharing in the benefits of oil spending and increased employment. In fact in the last five years the oil industry has increased the number employed in western Canada by over 10,000 workers, and the number is growing rapidly year by year. The hopes of Alberta are bright that the province will become one of Canada's great industrial provinces because of oil and gas and the by-products of petroleum and gas.
As most of you know, a $50 million plant is now under construction at Edmonton to turn out a broad range of petrochemicals from the rich gases obtained from the refining of Alberta crude oil. At Fort Saskatchewan a new plant under construction will use Alberta gas to refine nickel ores brought from Manitoba. Sulphur plants are being built at Turner valley and Jumping Pound near Calgary. Alberta has become a major oil refining area. One thing that is not yet sufficiently realized in my home province is that gas export will make available from the raw gas a host of liquid and solid by-products that can be used in Alberta to turn out plastics, synthetic rubber, fabrics, detergents and many other products of the petrochemical industry. In other words, in my opinion gas export will help to speed the industrial growth of my home province.
